With no money for ads, she sent DMs one by one: an Instagram message to Elena George at Good Morning America, a LinkedIn message to April Franzino at Good Housekeeping. She LinkedIn-messaged more than 20 editors; only one replied, and even after replying it was six months before they met. The first print coverage came out in July 2015 — just a very small slot in Good Housekeeping. Her logic: do it one person at a time, because you never know who will change your life.

28:41 During those seven viral days, the company had no employees
Before Black Friday 2016, she shot an ad on an iPhone about Infinity Waterproof Eyeliner, customers started commenting on their own, and the business took off. She called her sister to say they'd do $5,000 that day, then $25,000 the next, and within seven days $100,000. At that point the company had not a single employee: her friend Megan, a dental hygienist, came after work to do customer service; her sister did customer service on her lunch break; her mom came too. The first official hires came from Christy's sorority at the University of Washington — women five years younger than Carissa who had never met Christy, but knew Thrive and its mission.

32:56 Failing to raise money is what preserved control
From 2013 to 2015 she spent a lot of time fundraising, very unsuccessfully. Only after the company was already profitable, with revenue above $30 million, did she take capital — and she only needed a few hundred thousand dollars for inventory. Because she wasn't desperate for money, her negotiating position was completely different: she and her lawyer wrote the term sheet themselves, kept majority equity and control of the company, and no one else could decide whether she sold it. Her advice is to raise less, because scarcity keeps that focused mindset. She also says that if she had gotten more money than she could spend early on, she might have lost that focus and never polished the products one at a time.

36:31 Mission runs repeat purchase; product runs survival
People always ask her: mission or product? Her answer is product — it has to be product. Mission and product are bound together: because they donate to cancer patients, there are thousands of ingredients they will never use. But she's equally clear that customers don't come for the mission — they come because Liquid Lash Extensions won Allure's best of beauty, the Grammys of beauty. If the formula and the product don't give customers a solution, you're dead. Anyone who wants to donate can just write a check to a local charity; Thrive's value is letting people do two things at once.

40:48 Don't own the factory, own the formula
She believes no one needs to own their own manufacturing facility; the most important thing is owning your formulas. Ownership comes from creation, so they invest in their own cosmetic chemists. Then you negotiate exclusivity — those two things protect the formula and its integrity. She also stresses not to do deals on a handshake: have contracts, and reinforce them repeatedly, because once a product takes off it attracts competition. She says she likes competition because it keeps the team sharp, but she always keeps her eye on one question: what do our customers want from us.

42:57 Every product has to fund the next one
Thrive is self-funded and has always been profitable, so every product has to pay for the next one. She gives a very concrete example: if Empower Shine, a lipstick in development for years, doesn't sell well enough, they can't launch Lasting Mark Lip Stain, which they hope to bring out within a month. The skincare line, though developed with dermatologists, oncologists and ophthalmologists, is still small relative to the whole business. She sees complexion and sun care as opportunities, but a brand is built one product at a time, and that discipline can't be relaxed.

44:00 She says plainly she doesn't want to sell the company
Asked whether she'd be willing to be acquired by a big company the way Tatcha was, she says flatly no, I don't want to sell the company, and they've had the chance. She sees the ending as continuing to show up and keep developing products that change people's lives. She says she now has more money than she needs, so she can give it away; more important is how to leave the world better than she found it, and how to build a sustainable business that outlives them. She believes staying private is the best way, and growing people from within — for example, someone who started as a cosmetic chemistry intern is now a product development manager, and she hopes one day she'll run the whole company.

item.title: A University Endowment CIO: Fund Lives Are Too Long, and GPs and Our Math Don't Line Up
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-twentyvc-大学捐赠基金-cio-基金年限太长-gp-和我们的数学根本不一致/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-twentyvc-大学捐赠基金-cio-基金年限太长-gp-和我们的数学根本不一致/
item.description: The only reason private markets exist is to make money — but 15-to-18-year fund lives put GP incentives out of sync with endowment compounding math. What you should chase isn't the return multiple, it's the velocity of capital.
item.content:encoded:
The only reason private markets exist is to make money — but 15-to-18-year fund lives put GP incentives out of sync with endowment compounding math. What you should chase isn't the return multiple, it's the velocity of capital.

An extremely rare LP view: a CIO of a $2.6 billion endowment says plainly what's wrong with fund lives, platform funds and private credit, and explains how he bought the dip when software stocks crashed.

14:31 Fund lives are too long, and GP and LP math don't line up
David says he has no problem with VC itself, but he's ‘a little confused’ about fund lives: it used to be 10 to 12 years, now it's 15 to 18. He runs the numbers — an 18-year fund that goes up 15x sounds great, but roll that into three 6-year growth equity funds each going up 3x and compounding, and over 18 years you get 27x, roughly double. So the issue isn't the return multiple, it's the ‘velocity of capital’. He stresses that students can't pay tuition with a return multiple, only with dollars, so what he wants is to maximize the pile of money, and maximizing that pile is determined by simple compounding math.

17:38 Talking returns without time is saying nothing at all
David says there's a rule in the office: you're not allowed to talk about returns without talking about time. Because in private markets everyone is used to saying ‘you're up 2x, 3x, 5x’, but that's no information at all — 5x over 30 years is a disaster, 5x over 5 months is a miracle. He ties this rule to ‘velocity of capital’: once velocity starts asymptotically approaching its ceiling, it's time to exit and move to the next target. He also admits this is out of step with GP interests: the GP has winners in hand, the companies are still running, and a 6x on paper raises the next fund better than a 3x — but that's the GP's business decision, not the objective he's optimizing for.

21:43 When software stocks crashed, he judged by making calls, not by models
In early 2026 software stocks got killed, and the market narrative was ‘software is dead, everything goes to zero, anyone can vibe code a replacement’. David says he's not an engineer and a lot of Silicon Valley is beyond his understanding, but he understands how people decide. He called friends who run private family businesses with three to five hundred employees and asked, ‘if your son-in-law vibe codes something, are you going to rip out your CRM?’ The answer was ‘not in a million years’. He also cites the Salesforce CEO saying AI at best reaches 93% accuracy — but software demands 100%, the books have to balance. His conclusion: in these vertical industries, software may actually be the delivery vehicle for AI, because the trust software vendors have already built translates into ‘can you add AI features on top of your software’.

23:44 He admits he can't tell the baby from the bathwater, so he gives the money to people who can
Software stocks were then at a 40-50% discount to October 2025. David's judgment was that ‘the baby is being thrown out with the bathwater’, but he openly admits he doesn't know which is the baby and which is the bathwater. His approach isn't to pick stocks himself, it's to give managers more money while asking them to ‘go through the list, tell me which are least likely to be disrupted by AI, and then overweight those’. He positions himself as an allocator: he makes allocation decisions based on judgments about human behavior, but relies on managers to provide ground truth in their areas of expertise. This is also what he keeps stressing — they spend more time on asset allocation than on picking managers.

26:47 Public markets are more rational than private ones, because tens of millions of people are pricing
David doesn't think public markets are a casino. His argument: private valuations work by three people sitting in a room saying ‘I think it's worth X’, then someone says ‘I'll invest at that price’, and the whole price gets reset. Public markets are traded every day by tens of millions of people on information, so they ‘incorporate all available information’ — that doesn't mean they're right, for example they've decided Elon Musk himself is a premium and SpaceX should be worth $1.8 trillion, but that's a different thing from three people making the call in private. He says explicitly that public market prices are more legitimate than private ones, no question about it.

34:59 Buying the dip isn't about drawing lines: invest a tranche for every 10% drop
David's mechanism is very specific: if the market drops 0 to 10% they don't care, they treat it as normal fluctuation. He trains young analysts with a discounted-goods analogy — would you rush to the store for 10% off? What about 30% off? 40% off? They slice declines into 10% tranches and keep liquidity ready, investing one tranche for every 10% drop. So there's no line-drawing behavior like ‘it's down 20%, I'm going all in’; instead it's down 20%, invest 20%; down 30%, invest another 20%; down 40%, another 20%. He admits this means you can never be fully invested before the rebound, effectively leaving money on the table, but what you get in return is never ending up in the position of ‘I love this asset so much, it keeps falling, and I have no money left to add’.

49:30 If a manager changes their game, replace them — even if they're making money
David uses a baseball GM analogy: I hired a third baseman, a shortstop and a second baseman based on batting average and fielding percentage, but if I walk onto the field and find two people standing at second base, the third baseman has to go — ‘I don't care what your return is’. He says explicitly that if the market changed, you changed with it and did well and made me money, but your positions no longer match what we're trying to do, we won't re-up. What he demands isn't that you never change, it's that you talk to him before you change: ‘What makes you think you can do this, when we have no data showing you're good at it?’ He also distinguishes two kinds of change: moving from Series B to late-stage Series A doesn't matter, but moving from ‘investing in companies with product-market fit’ to ‘investing in two people in a garage who don't yet know if they can build anything’ is not okay.

57:44 The real bottleneck for data centers has shifted from power to permits
David says the AI rebound is happening at the data center layer, and in his region rather than Silicon Valley. He lays out an evolution: five or six years ago the most valuable thing in data centers was land, then it was ‘land with power’, and now it's ‘land with permits and power’. The reason is that permit boards are elected by local residents, residents plant signs on their own lawns in opposition, and anyone who wants re-election has to say no. The data center parcels in his book rose 50% in six months. He also mentions something happening right now: permitted owners are starting to get calls from utilities saying they can supply power earlier than planned. He judges that power prices will keep rising over the next five to seven years, until power dispatch is no longer constrained by supply.

item.title: Home Depot Has the Best Return Since IPO, and It Isn't From Selling Cheap
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-acquired-home-depot-上市以来回报第一-靠的不是卖便宜货/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-acquired-home-depot-上市以来回报第一-靠的不是卖便宜货/
item.description: It packaged education into retail: a customer asks how to fix something, and the associate stops and teaches. A 25-cent washer leads to a $100,000 kitchen remodel, and that kind of value can't be managed with a Six Sigma spreadsheet.
item.content:encoded:
It packaged education into retail: a customer asks how to fix something, and the associate stops and teaches. A 25-cent washer leads to a $100,000 kitchen remodel, and that kind of value can't be managed with a Six Sigma spreadsheet.

A three-and-a-half-hour retail case study: the first half is 1970s financial engineering and startup gossip, the second half is a mechanism teardown of decentralization versus centralization and stock-based incentives, at high information density.

1:08 North America only, yet worth more than Netflix
Home Depot has a market cap of $350 billion, the 45th-largest public company in the world, worth more than Netflix, Alibaba, Goldman Sachs and LVMH. David stresses how crazy that is, because unlike those other companies, it only does North America. Ben admits he had it wrong at first — he thought home improvement was just a big store in the middle of a shopping center, not a company that mattered to the world. The category is far bigger than he thought, and nearly all of its revenue comes from one continent.

2:16 Since its 1981 IPO, it's the S&P 500's top return
Home Depot went public in 1981, a year after Apple. If you had put $1,000 into each and held to today, Home Depot's return would beat Apple's; with dividends reinvested, that's roughly 25% compounded annually over 45 years. It is the single best-performing stock in the S&P 500 from its listing date to today: $1,000 would become about $17 million, versus just $170,000 for the S&P 500 over the same period. David notes that who holds this equity is itself a key part of the company's strategy — early employee ownership and long-term share price growth are the same mechanism.

42:12 Home Depot is not a Price Club clone
What Bernie set out to build was not a low-SKU warehouse club but a warehouse where you buy everything for one job: Price Club carried only 4,000 SKUs, while Home Depot would stock 25,000 and deal with a huge number of suppliers. Gross margin was set below the industry too — hardware retail's standard was 45% at the time, and they ran at 30%. Another fundamental difference is the nature of the goods: anyone will buy toilet paper, but nobody is born knowing how to build a deck, install blinds or lay flooring, so the store has to be staffed with people who have real expertise — and Price Club's org structure was never designed for that.

1:26:09 Big-box stores aren't the moat; service is
In the 1980s a pile of capital rushed into the category: Builders Square, Home Club, Home Quarters Warehouse, Mr. HOW Warehouse, all copying Home Depot, and today not one of them is left. David's explanation: Home Depot is not "Costco selling hardware." Costco is general merchandise retail, where customers need no human help beyond the checkout lane; Home Depot is specialty retail, where price, selection and convenience — the "trinity" — aren't enough, and you also have to offer something unique to the category, just as a tire shop has to mount tires, a beauty store has to let you try makeup, and Apple has to have a Genius Bar. Home Depot essentially invented "serving the customer" in the home improvement category itself.

1:35:12 Low gross margin runs on turns, not margin rate
Home Depot's warehouse model has two structural disadvantages: an extremely high SKU count and an extremely large in-store service staff, which makes rapid turnover operationally hard, and per-store labor costs higher than the price club model. Ben says what holds it all up is "manufacturing buying frenzy" — with that many SKUs, you have to give people a reason to buy them all. The key line: what feeds the company is not the gross margin percentage, it's gross margin dollars. So it needs enough volume and fast enough turns that the gross margin dollars add up to justify the store carrying all that inventory. Once volume is there, it can place bigger orders with suppliers, demand lower prices, and pass the savings to customers, spinning the whole wheel faster.

1:53:38 It invented the national chain, so no one could buy nationally
Home Depot's early philosophy was radical decentralization, letting stores use local knowledge to decide what to stock and how much, which Bernie estimated lifted per-store sales 15% to 20%. But at scale, the costs of decentralization outweighed the benefits: operational chaos, systems and technology that couldn't be unified, and countless decision-makers and negotiators facing the same suppliers, unable to get the best prices. Ben points out a key thing: this problem didn't exist for anyone else, because the very concept of a "national hardware chain" was invented by Home Depot — before it, nobody bought nationally, so there was no national buying opportunity to have.

2:12:04 Replacing knowledgeable staff with 16-year-old cashiers
Nardelli replaced a large share of floor staff with part-time general-retail labor, effectively killing the whole philosophy of "a knowledgeable person sells you a 25-cent washer, fixes your sink, and brings the big follow-on order." According to Arvind's research, from 2000 to 2006 store staff fell from 200 to 170, a 15% cut. Store manager standards changed too, with a preference for college-educated candidates — while the associates hired in the stores had no college degrees, effectively telling those people they were locked into jobs with no promotion path. The result: customer satisfaction fell to the lowest among major U.S. retailers, while revenue and profit doubled.

2:20:10 Pay not tied to the stock price means no value stored in the company
Ben nails the incentive misalignment: if pay is tied to the stock price, you don't care about current-period results — you want investors to believe you're storing long-term value in the company, so you keep prices low, push volume up, and make customers fanatical; if pay is tied to today's numbers, you don't store value in the company, you just think about pumping today's numbers. David calls it "the paradoxical misalignment of incentives." Nardelli refused to tie any of his pay to the stock price, on the grounds that the stock price was the one metric he couldn't control — which cut directly against the core of the company model: the associate's promise had always been "I do good work, the stock goes up, I get rich."

item.title: A Soviet Spy's Secret Shame Nearly Stopped World War III
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-historyhit-一个苏联间谍的难言之隐-差点阻止了第三次世界大战/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-historyhit-一个苏联间谍的难言之隐-差点阻止了第三次世界大战/
item.description: In 1981, a senior KGB officer in Tehran walked into MI6 and offered to spy — not for money or ideology, but because he believed the West could cure his erectile dysfunction. The intelligence he handed over led the US and Britain to give the Soviets' coup plan to the Iranians.
item.content:encoded:
In 1981, a senior KGB officer in Tehran walked into MI6 and offered to spy — not for money or ideology, but because he believed the West could cure his erectile dysfunction. The intelligence he handed over led the US and Britain to give the Soviets' coup plan to the Iranians.

Ben Macintyre tells a Cold War spy story that has never been told, with astonishing detail and tight pacing — though the information density is concentrated in the second half, on the coup and its aftermath, while the setup runs long.

0:00 A spy story that has never been told
Ben Macintyre's new book Redwood tells a Cold War story that had never been made public before: in 1981, a senior KGB officer in Tehran, Vladimir Kuzichkin, walked into MI6 and offered to spy, becoming a double agent codenamed "Redwood." The intelligence he provided revealed that the Soviets were planning a coup through the Iranian communist Tudeh Party to overthrow Khomeini's government, after which the Red Army would cross into Iran from Afghanistan, Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan. The Pentagon's response plan was a nuclear strike — because conventional forces were not enough to stop a full Soviet invasion. What makes the story so strange is that Kuzichkin's motive for defecting was intensely personal: he suffered from erectile dysfunction and believed Western medicine could cure him.

3:01 1981 came closer to nuclear war than the Cuban Missile Crisis
Ben Macintyre points out that 1981 was one of the closest moments of nuclear confrontation in the Cold War, second only to the Cuban Missile Crisis. After the Iranian Revolution, every faction — nationalists, liberals, communists and Islamists — was fighting for power, and Tehran became a "seething cauldron of spies." The CIA, MI6 and the KGB all poured in at once. The Soviets had just invaded Afghanistan and were making good progress, while the US was desperate to re-establish a foothold in the Middle East. If the Soviets took Iran, they could control warm-water ports and oil fields and win the Cold War. So the Pentagon was already drawing up nuclear response plans, including using portable nuclear weapons to blow up mountain ranges and block Soviet armored columns.

8:18 The CIA was blind in Tehran; MI6 broke the rules and kept a man there
After the Iran hostage crisis, the CIA was thrown out of Tehran, had no human intelligence in Iran at all, and knew nothing about a possible Soviet coup. The only service still capable of operating was MI6, but Britain's condition for maintaining a diplomatic mission in 1981 was "no spying of any kind." MI6 nevertheless sent Ian McCready in under commercial counselor cover — a huge gamble by the British government. McCready's instructions were "do nothing, recruit no one, keep a low profile" — because if he were caught, the Iranians would take the entire embassy hostage. He could only communicate with London using a World War II-era cipher machine called RockX, which was extremely cumbersome to operate and of which only two existed in the world.

12:29 His motive for defecting was impotence, not money or ideology
Kuzichkin was a senior officer at the KGB residency in Tehran, in charge of illegal spy programs across the entire Middle East, and the only defector who understood how the illegal system worked. He walked into MI6 on his own and offered to spy for the West. The intelligence world has an acronym, MICE — money, ideology, coercion, ego — but Kuzichkin fit none of the categories. He was partly driven by alienation from the regime, but the root cause was this: he suffered from erectile dysfunction and believed the West had a drug that could cure it. He had just married, loved his wife deeply, and could not reveal the secret to his KGB colleagues or to Soviet doctors. McCready did not mock him or exploit him; he took him with extreme seriousness, even sending MI6 headquarters an unprecedented telex: "Help. What do I do with a spy who has erectile dysfunction?"

21:52 He photographed every KGB file in the Middle East
For nearly a year, McCready ran Kuzichkin with old-fashioned tradecraft: dead drops, brush contacts, a miniature camera. He gave Kuzichkin a Minox miniature camera to carry into the office every day and photograph every document he could get his hands on. In the end the Redwood archive filled four truckloads. MI6 gave him the codename "Redwood" — because he was six foot four, and because they could not resist the pun: Red for communism, Wood for his "problem." Kuzichkin's core intelligence was this: the Soviets were planning a coup through the Tudeh Party, the money and weapons were already in place, the Tudeh had a secret military underground, and Kuzichkin himself was the coordinator between the KGB and the Tudeh.

29:05 The US and Britain handed the coup plan to the Iranians
After Kuzichkin escaped to Britain, MI6 debated internally whether to use the intelligence. Chris Cohn, who ran the operations directorate and later became chief of MI6, argued it had to be used. He said that if they did not use it, intelligence about a Tudeh communist coup was meaningless. So MI6 sent Redwood to Islamabad, Pakistan, under diplomatic cover, to meet Iranian intelligence. The meeting lasted three days, Kuzichkin laid everything out, and MI6 handed the Iranians all four truckloads of intelligence. It was also an attempt to open a secret channel to Iran at a time when Tehran's relations with the West were dire. It was deeply illegal, and if it had come out it would have been a huge scandal — the British and American governments acting to protect the Islamic Revolution.

31:05 Iran used the intelligence to execute eight thousand communists
Once the Revolutionary Guard had the intelligence, within two months it arrested eight thousand Iranian communists, about half of whom were executed. This became a cornerstone of Iran's modern theocratic state. From that moment on, Khomeini tolerated no opposition at all; everyone was purged, including people already in prison, and it turned into a massacre. It also reinforced two convictions of the Islamic Revolution: first, that all opposition must be destroyed, because fifth columns were everywhere; second, that whatever happened, the British were behind it. MI6 and the CIA inadvertently consolidated the Iranian regime and created a monster — almost an exact replay of Afghanistan, where money poured in to Islamic guerrillas fighting the Soviets and ultimately produced al-Qaeda, ISIS and 9/11.

38:11 History is often driven by perceptions, not facts
Ben Macintyre stresses that it cannot be known whether the Soviets would actually have carried out the coup, but everyone involved believed they would. McCready believed it, Kuzichkin believed it, and MI6, the CIA, the KGB and the Tudeh themselves all believed it. That was enough — nuclear war can break out on the basis of perception rather than fact, and the Cuban Missile Crisis was the same. Would Khrushchev really have used those weapons? We do not know, but everyone believed he might. The story was never told because everyone involved did not want it told: the Iranians did not, because it meant the West had outsmarted them again; the KGB did not, because it was a humiliation — they had failed to spot the defector, 18 Soviet diplomats were expelled from Iran as a result, the entire Tudeh operation was dismantled, and agent networks across the Middle East and even in Canada were exposed.

item.title: After You Die, What's Left Isn't the Cause of Death — It's the Version of You Other People Assemble
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-tal-死后你留下的不是死因-是别人拼凑的你/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-tal-死后你留下的不是死因-是别人拼凑的你/
item.description: All three stories do the same thing: once a person is dead, the people left behind can only reconstruct someone who can no longer speak from fragments — texts, obituaries, Facebook comments — and the version they piece together often bears no resemblance to how the person saw themselves.
item.content:encoded:
All three stories do the same thing: once a person is dead, the people left behind can only reconstruct someone who can no longer speak from fragments — texts, obituaries, Facebook comments — and the version they piece together often bears no resemblance to how the person saw themselves.

A narrative show, no data or mechanisms, but each of the three stories has a twist, and the second story's twist is the most valuable. Medium information density, good for the commute.

5:12 After you die, other people will get you wrong
As a kid, Graham was playing on a seesaw at a construction site and dropped a 25-pound curbstone from second-story height, trying to launch a brick off the other end. The brick didn't fly — it shot straight at his face and grazed past his hair. He survived, but decades later what he keeps thinking about isn't the terror of that second, it's something else: if the brick had actually killed him, how would a coroner have read the scene? A brick, a seesaw, a kid — could they have pieced together the truth? That's where the show lays out the premise of the whole episode — death itself isn't the hardest part; the hard part is the judgment other people make about who you were after you're gone.

12:15 She has now outlived her sister
Nadia wrote a long letter to the drug dealer who killed her sister. The sharpest cut in it isn't anger, it's arithmetic: at 6:49 p.m. on March 11, 2018, she outlived her sister's age — she had spent a few more seconds in this world than the sister who was two and a half years older. She says it makes no sense, that he bent the universe crooked. She went through her sister's phone, read the texts, listened to the voicemails, trying to figure out the life her sister had stopped sharing with her. She even admits she needs this dealer: because of him, she can say "if it weren't for that person," and she doesn't have to hate her sister, or hate herself.

20:28 The message she never answered became the last one
A few days before her sister died, her sister sent an unimportant text asking if she remembered the little stick-figure illustration labeled faible (weak) in their middle-school French textbook. It was an old joke between the sisters. Nadia was still angry about their last fight and deliberately didn't reply, wanting to punish her. But a strong thought surfaced: you don't want this to be the last message she ever sends you. She still didn't reply. After her sister died, she found a text her sister had sent a friend that night: "How do I stop hating my sister? My family really hates me." The friend replied: "Damn, Nadia the snitch." When she saw the word "hate" next to her own name, she felt hollowed out.

33:53 He lived to read his own eulogies
Comedian Dave Marr fell into a diabetic coma for a month. His friends thought he was going to be taken off life support; more than fifty people gathered at his house for a vigil, and his 1,700 Facebook friends started writing eulogies on his wall. Then his parents didn't pull the tube, he was transferred to another hospital, and he woke up. After recovering, he sat in his parents' basement and read from 2 a.m. to 3:30 a.m., getting through about a hundred eulogies. He read his brother's post trying to set the record straight, buried by the algorithm with only 70 likes, while the posts mourning him got double the likes. He read about someone remembering him kicking in a storage-room door at a party insisting it was the bathroom, about an ex-girlfriend thanking him for breaking up with her in the car because it was cold outside, about someone saying he "sweats unreasonably much."

42:06 The man in the eulogies was a stranger to him
After reading all the eulogies, Dave wasn't moved — he felt bad. The self he remembered was someone who shoplifted at Walgreens and spent a night in jail; the self in the eulogies was known by every Walgreens clerk, bought people free Chipotle, treated everyone as an equal. He says it's hard to square the image in his own head with the image people described when they thought he was dead. He insists the coma was his own doing — "it was my carelessness, my recklessness that got me here." Blake's side is a different story: he lost a friend and got him back, and now Dave's laugh is like music to him. The show says both men got a second chance, to love and to be loved, and the latter is much harder than the former.

57:33 Nobody mentioned how he died
Charlie, a retired Navy officer, went in a friend's place to the funeral of a SEAL he'd never met, Eddie Furlani. He couldn't find any reporting on the cause of death and assumed it was a training accident. At the funeral he noticed the back rows full of big men in three-piece suits and sunglasses, expressionless the whole time, until Eddie's seven-year-old daughter Zelma broke down crying and was taken out by her stepmother. After the service he called his friend to report back, and the friend said, "I'm glad someone came, I was worried no one would," then added, "because of the way he killed himself." Charlie says that moment was like grabbing a live wire — no reporting, no mention in the obituary, not a word in the eulogy.

59:47 The daughter was crying because she felt ashamed
The day before the interview, Charlie called Eddie's widow to confirm, and only then learned that Zelma had cried and asked to leave the funeral not out of grief but out of shame — she thought everyone knew her dad had killed himself, and that she was a bad person. Charlie says hearing this terrified him: a seven-year-old girl treating herself as an outcast because of her father's death, when the room was full of people who had come to support her. He also talks about service members losing their "larger mission" after they leave the military, and says he can probably put himself in Eddie's shoes and understand what he was thinking in that moment, but when asked whether he could say more, he stops and says he can't take on that subject.

1:02:00 He wanted to be the sound of that helicopter
Charlie has had suicidal thoughts himself; this ended his Navy career, and he only agreed to talk about it after the mic was off. The host asks whether he wrote the piece because Eddie's funeral might be his own future funeral, and he says no. He explains the real reason: on medevac flights he knew that the sound of the helicopter approaching alone could improve a dying person's vital signs. He says, I'm writing to you because I want to be that helicopter sound for someone. The show ends with the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline, 800-273-TALK.

item.title: The British Expedition to Abyssinia: An Emperor Seizes Every Diplomat
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-restishistory-英国远征阿比西尼亚-一个皇帝把外交官全扣了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-restishistory-英国远征阿比西尼亚-一个皇帝把外交官全扣了/
item.description: Victoria never answered one letter, so Tewodros II locked the British consul and a batch of missionaries inside Magdala at the top of a mountain — and got an expeditionary force instead.
item.content:encoded:
Victoria never answered one letter, so Tewodros II locked the British consul and a batch of missionaries inside Magdala at the top of a mountain — and got an expeditionary force instead.

The first half is a long build, but the second half is extraordinarily dense with the hostage crisis and the emperor's psychological collapse — good for listeners interested in imperial history and the game of negotiation.

0:00 One unanswered letter started the war
Tewodros II wrote a letter to Queen Victoria, phrased like a pen pal: ‘How are you? I am well, thank God.’ The letter travelled by way of the Red Sea, Aden, Bombay, Suez, Alexandria, Marseille and London, halfway around the world, and ended up filed by the Foreign Office in the India Office records. No one replied. The emperor waited two years, and his expectation turned to suspicion: he became convinced Britain was colluding with his Muslim enemies. In 1864 he seized the British consul Cameron and a group of missionaries, and the hostage crisis began.

10:21 He claimed descent from Solomon, and meant it
Abyssinia had a legend: a descendant of Solomon and David would rise, unify the divided kingdom, defeat the Egyptians, and march all the way to Jerusalem, and his name would be Tewodros. In 1855 Kassa, a man of obscure origins who had been a bandit chief, defeated his last rival and proclaimed himself the new emperor, taking the name Tewodros II. He later claimed to be of Solomon's line, though he said nothing of it when Plowden first met him. This messianic identity was both the source of his legitimacy and the root of his later paranoia.

21:46 After his wife died he began to lose control
In 1858 Tewodros's wife Tewabech died, and he was grief-stricken. His next wife, the 12-year-old Tiruwork, was cold to him and said, ‘I am speaking with a king greater than you — get out.’ He began drinking heavily, sleeping with women in the camp at random, and admitted to the missionaries that he was living ‘a very unchristian and indecent life.’ In 1860 his friend Plowden was ambushed by rebels and died nine days after being speared. Britain sent a new representative only two years later, and in the interval the emperor's paranoia deteriorated sharply.

26:55 The letter Cameron carried back became the fuse
At the end of 1862, when Cameron left the emperor's camp, he took with him a letter in which Tewodros asked Victoria to arrange safe passage for his envoys and said, ‘See how Islam oppresses the Christians.’ Cameron came back saying he had received no reply from London, and the emperor began to suspect he had gone off to Sudan to collude with the Muslims. In October 1863 the missionary Stern angered the emperor by publishing The Wanderings Among the Falashas, and was arrested, whipped and put in chains. In January 1864 Cameron and the other missionaries were also seized, and all the hostages realised the nightmare had only just begun.

39:33 What Britain really feared was France
The Foreign Office did not particularly care whether the missionaries lived or died; what worried them was France. Suez Canal fever was at its height, and if they alienated Tewodros he might turn to Paris, and France would then control the route from the Red Sea to India. So they sent Hormuzd Rassam — a Mosul-born Assyrian, archaeologist, discoverer of Ashurbanipal's palace and the Epic of Gilgamesh, Oxford-educated, a convert to Protestantism, and an ardent Anglophile. He set out for Abyssinia with a letter from Queen Victoria and two assistants, Dr. Blanc and Lieutenant Prideaux.

49:02 Rassam nearly succeeded, then was seized too
In January 1866 Rassam met Tewodros in his blue diplomatic uniform, and after reading Victoria's letter the emperor was so excited he could not sleep; the next day he dictated a reply calling the queen ‘the defender of the religion chosen by God.’ He agreed to release all the hostages, but demanded that Rassam first accompany him on a campaign to put down a rebellion. Along the way the emperor kept sending gifts: muskets, manuscripts, salmon, antelope, two lion cubs, two monkeys and a baboon. In March 1866 the hostages were finally brought to the lake, but on 13 April, when Rassam went to say goodbye, he found that he too had been arrested.

57:19 He held everyone just to get gunsmiths
Why did Tewodros seize Rassam? There are three possibilities: he had been acting all along; he was overcome at the last moment by his hatred of the missionaries; or he genuinely liked Rassam and could not bear to let him go. Philip Marsden thinks the third most likely — the emperor was infatuated with Rassam and saw him as his only channel to British friendship and British technology. The emperor then wrote to Victoria demanding that she send ‘skilled craftsmen, blacksmiths, gunsmiths, artillery experts’ to make guns, and said he would release the prisoners once he was satisfied.

1:02:28 In the cellar he admitted he was mad
Tewodros locked the missionaries in a cellar, came in with a bottle of arak, and sat down among them drinking and talking. At last he said, calmly and sadly: ‘My father was mad. People often said I was mad, and I never believed them. But now I know it is true.’ Rassam urged him not to say such things, and the emperor walked to the door, turned back, and said in a hoarse whisper: ‘I am mad. Goodbye.’ Then he left. For nearly two years afterwards they were held on the mountain top at Magdala, ten thousand feet up, in chains, their spines bent.

item.title: Compute flips from shortage to glut in 2027, and the AI bubble may not pop
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-asianometry-2027-年算力会从短缺变成过剩-ai-泡沫未必破/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-asianometry-2027-年算力会从短缺变成过剩-ai-泡沫未必破/
item.description: Usable AI data center capacity is about 15 GW at the end of 2026 and races to 45-55 GW by the end of 2027, a 30-40 GW increment. At $50 billion of revenue per gigawatt, the two giants would have to produce $750 billion to $1.5 trillion, and that number does not hold up.
item.content:encoded:
Usable AI data center capacity is about 15 GW at the end of 2026 and races to 45-55 GW by the end of 2027, a 30-40 GW increment. At $50 billion of revenue per gigawatt, the two giants would have to produce $750 billion to $1.5 trillion, and that number does not hold up.

The first half is on-the-ground reporting from Hot Chips and Semicon Taiwan; the second half is the real value of this episode: a bottom-up arithmetic of compute supply and demand, plus the judgment that anti-AI sentiment could swing elections.

3:05 The window for new AI chips has reopened
The author wrote last year that ‘the window for new AI chips has closed, except for Google's TPU’, and here he explicitly takes it back and says he was wrong. The trigger was OpenAI unveiling its in-house chip Jalapeno at Hot Chips, a short talk with high information density. Outside the hall a ring of new AI chip startups was gathered: Etched, MatX, Posetron, Fractile. Etched gave no talk but built presence by handing out hats and having its founder ask questions all over the Q&A. The author reminds us these are hardware companies: they do not just design chips, they have to build their own racks and systems and get into the lab and do the work, and recruiting top talent and execution are hard barriers. His survival test borrows Nathan Bedford Forrest's controversial line: get there first, and with the most men.

6:08 Semicon Taiwan is really TSMC's request for proposals
First-timers are surprised: neither TSMC nor ASML has a booth. But TSMC dominates the whole show — its teams walk the hall visiting new suppliers and scouting new technology, and many information sessions have TSMC executives on stage laying the company's problems out in public. The author's conclusion is that Semicon Taiwan is essentially an RFP that TSMC issues to the entire semiconductor industry. The technical throughline is clear: future manufacturing has to go big. AI chips are hitting existing limits, most typically the reticle limit, which determines how large an area a lithography machine can print. TSMC had a slide showing they are preparing to build a ‘battleship-class’ chip spanning 14 reticles, and the industry's response speed is as fast as ever.

7:10 Glass panel packaging has gone from PPT to the show floor
Two years ago the author made a video on panel level packaging, which was the theme of Semicon Taiwan 2024, when it was still all talks and slideshows. Now AI systems are so large that the industry wants to use square, glass panel interposers to carry chiplets and memory in place of silicon interposers. The author's attitude is reserved: can TSMC make them without warping or cracking? ‘I'll believe it when I see the chips.’ But the ecosystem is already moving, and equipment such as handling robots adapted to square panels has appeared in the hall. He judges this wave of ‘chipmaxing’ will be one of the most far-reaching technology transitions in semiconductor history, roughly on the scale of the move to 300 mm wafers.

8:12 The spot market has vanished, and VCs now help portfolio companies find GPUs
When the author was last in the Bay Area in September 2025 the picture was completely different. Since then long-running agentic AI has swept Silicon Valley, triggered in part by stronger models such as Anthropic's Opus 4.5 around November 2025 and by Open Claw. In February 2026 prices started rising, everyone scrambled to lock in compute, and Anthropic led the way signing big deals with SpaceX, Google and others. The author was told that by the time of this trip the spot market had completely vanished. For Neoclouds (a term coined by semi-analyst Dan Nishbal in April 2024 for pure cloud vendors that resell AI training and inference compute, such as Coreweave and Nebius) this is a huge boon, and they are confident the shortage will last at least another one to two years. The author met several people who did not know each other and each wanted to start a Neocloud. For AI startups this is a business risk: imagine telling investors your product has to wait until mid-2027 because there is not enough compute. The new way VCs help portfolio companies is to go find compute, and he heard of people scraping together a thousand GPUs and hunting in unexpected places like Eastern Europe.

9:12 Two giants are feasting while compute still goes to waste
By contrast, Anthropic and OpenAI are feasting internally. Dylan recently said on Dashpod that these two AI giants each have about 5 GW of compute. The author infers from this that a considerable share of all that compute may be wasted, and anecdotes he heard confirm this ‘rolling in it’ is not being used as efficiently as possible. He also asked every AI insider he talked to one question: will Google return to the frontier? The general consensus is no, though the explanations are vague. Several people pointed out that Google's decision to sell a large amount of compute to Anthropic is itself an admission that it does not believe it either. This is a big reversal from the period when Gemini 3 made some people think OpenAI was finished. What the author heard is that Google suffered severe talent drain, plus a culture unfavourable to frontier AI.

11:15 Neolabs are venture capital that treats compute as money
What fascinates the author most is the Neolab: a research startup with basically no revenue that raises money to explore an interesting AI idea, whose founders are often elite researchers and whose business plan is little more than ‘discover a completely new architecture’. The most famous and earliest, Safe Superintelligence, raised a billion dollars and has still released no product or model. The label is fuzzy, covering recursive intelligence, Humans, Core Automation, Flapping Airplanes and others; among those with products are Japan's Sakana AI, Thinking Machines, Reflection AI, plus a batch in verticals such as materials science, world models and robotics. The first reaction is that these assets are dumb: no revenue, no plan to monetise soon. But the author can understand it: historically breakthrough science came from research universities, government labs or Bell Labs, and now university funding is being cut and talent is being sucked into industry; AI is probably the first major technology in the past 50 years to emerge without government involvement, and in this era research is closed and secretive. So let Nvidia, holding compute and cash, plus a pile of VCs, fund these asymmetric bets. OpenAI and Anthropic are locked into the transformer paradigm and are unlikely to spend on researching these directions. The probability of failure is high, but most of the money was given in the form of compute anyway; if someone really strikes gold and forces the giants to pivot (say, to a more data-efficient architecture), the giants will most likely buy the discoverer at an eye-watering price, and one such deal pays for everything. The author thinks this is a better use of cash than continuing buybacks, and names Apple.

14:15 Tokens are burning and nobody has measured ROI
Customers really are burning tokens, but are they getting ROI? The author asked across the ecosystem and the answer is still vague: don't know, nobody has measured it, it is all anecdotal. He believes lower barriers to coding will hit knowledge work — financial firms used to hire a pile of reporting analysts to keep management on top of positions, and now two smart young analysts plus Claude writing a dashboard is enough, which he has seen with his own eyes. But for other AI capabilities, such as making spreadsheets or making presentations, the things marketing usually pushes, he has seen no obvious impact. Maybe it just needs more time, maybe it is a problem of intelligence itself. OpenAI recently published a blog on how agents accelerate internal research, but still positions AI capability at intern level: able to execute routine tasks, still far from a real AI researcher. What he heard is that AI still lacks human research taste, though some believe sufficient scale can achieve it. And one thing holds for everyone in San Francisco: people are working harder than before. If the models are really that capable, why does everyone say they have more work? Maybe AI does not kill our work for us, it gives us more work.

15:17 Compute flips from shortage to glut in 2027
Everyone says shortage, shortage, two more years of shortage, and the author instead suspects things will not go as expected. His arithmetic is not complicated: usable AI data center capacity at the end of 2026 is estimated at about 15 GW, with OpenAI and Anthropic each taking about 5 GW; the supply chain will respond, and by the end of 2027 that number is estimated to reach 45-55 GW, an increment of 30-40 GW, of which the two giants take about 30 GW. Assume half goes to training, leaving 15 GW combined for inference. Inference is currently modelled at about $50 billion of revenue per gigawatt (a figure from Dylan Patel on Dashpod), and it can also be reverse-engineered from Anthropic's deal to buy 300 MW from SpaceX for $1.25 billion a month; Dylan thinks smarter models can eventually push it to $100 billion per gigawatt. On that basis the two should produce $750 billion to $1.5 trillion of revenue in 2027. The author says that number is absurd: most people agree the two will do $150-200 billion this year, and next year he can just about imagine $400-500 billion, but $750 billion to $1.5 trillion is ‘two Walmarts’ or ‘two Toyotas’, barely credible, and he does not think it will happen. He bets revenue per gigawatt is far below $100 billion or even $50 billion, possibly only a small fraction of it. From the infrastructure side it looks the same: assume 40 GW lands in 2027, current rent is about $20 million per megawatt, implying a 3-year payback, so those 40 GW require $800 billion paid to infrastructure providers, in 2027 alone. He does not think that can be collected either, which means rents have to fall and someone somewhere has to take a loss. Conclusion: in 2027 the supply chain will deliver a lot of compute, most of it in the second half, and he bets this pushes the market from shortage to glut. He stresses he is not saying the AI bubble will pop, only that we will soon be flooded with compute — 2026 is agentic demand matched against 2025 supply, supply will catch up and probably overshoot; but after that maybe the next stage of growth ignites and demand balloons again, for example persistent AI.

item.title: Stalin Was Just the Bookkeeper in the Revolution, and Then He Became General Secretary
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-empirehist-斯大林在革命里只是个管账的-后来却成了总书记/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-empirehist-斯大林在革命里只是个管账的-后来却成了总书记/
item.description: In 1917, while Lenin and Trotsky were on the streets calling for insurrection, Stalin was doing the organizing and fundraising nobody else wanted. He became General Secretary later not by speeches, but by sitting at the table.
item.content:encoded:
In 1917, while Lenin and Trotsky were on the streets calling for insurrection, Stalin was doing the organizing and fundraising nobody else wanted. He became General Secretary later not by speeches, but by sitting at the table.

This episode covers the groundwork before Stalin took power: Georgian origins, seminary, a failed bank robbery. Medium information density, but it makes clear why he was able to rise.

5:28 Even his birthday was something he changed himself
The parish register, the seminary certificate, the tsarist police file and his own handwritten questionnaire from the 1920s all say 18 December 1878. But the birthday he announced once in power was 21 December 1879 — a year and three days off. Bob Service offers one judgment in his biography: forgery was too easy for him. Service also has an unprovable but persuasive conjecture — that changing the birthday helped him dodge conscription when he was young. The thing itself is the theme of the whole episode: this man's attitude toward facts was instrumental.

6:35 How anomalous it was for a Georgian to become master of Moscow
His real name was Joseph Jugashvili, and he was born in Georgia. Georgia is in the Caucasus, next to Armenia, just north of Iran and Turkey, far from Russia; it has its own language, its own alphabet, and its religion is Georgian Orthodoxy, which is not the same thing as Russian Orthodoxy. The analogy the episode gives is this: a man of Georgian Orthodox background climbing to the top of power in Moscow is like a mid-20th-century man of Irish Catholic background, from some remote place like Limerick, becoming master of London. For Georgians at the time, being ruled from Moscow meant being colonized.

8:43 His father refused to change trades, and then started hitting people
His father Bessarion (nicknamed Besso) was a cobbler with his own workshop in Gori, and by most accounts a good craftsman. But he refused to keep up with the times: he went on making Georgian-style soft leather high boots while the market had already turned to European shoes. He did not adapt; he became bitter and alcoholic, and the violence fell mainly on his wife Ekaterina (Kiki) and little Joseph, who was nicknamed "Crazy Besso." Stalin later told his daughter Svetlana one scene: his father was drunk and beating his mother, he grabbed a knife and threw it at his father, missed, his father charged, and he ran to a neighbor's house and hid there for several days until his father's rage passed.

11:52 Smallpox, a carriage, and a left arm that was too short
Around age six he caught smallpox, severe enough that his mother thought he would die — two older brothers had already died in infancy, and the family was too poor to afford a doctor, so they could only call a local folk healer. He survived, but his face was permanently scarred, and every official photograph was retouched. Later a runaway carriage hit him and broke his arm; the left arm never healed properly and was noticeably shorter and stiffer for the rest of his life. The episode's formulation is: smallpox did not take him, his father's violence did not take him, and the carriage did not take him either. His mother was extremely devoted to him and had ambitious plans for him.

16:07 He wrote poetry, and he was good at it
Two things happened at once in his late teens: he began writing rather good poetry, and he entered the seminary. The episode reads one poem: "The pink buds have already opened, toward the pale violet violets; brushed by the breeze, the lily of the valley bends over the grass. Flowers, my Georgia. May peace come to my native land, and may you, friends, make our homeland famous through study." Anita says that in the original Georgian it is quite beautiful. It shows two things: he was a proud Georgian, not a Russian; and in the tsarist context, this way of writing about a "homeland" was already close to sedition.

19:09 The seminary was the tsar's Russification machine
In 1894 he won a place at the Tiflis Theological Seminary. The sign over the school said Georgian Orthodox, but in practice it was under the control of the Russian Orthodox Church, one of the institutions the tsar used to "Russify" the borderlands. Students were kept under close surveillance, and reports were written constantly: were these people good subjects of the tsar, were they talking sedition. And right under that surveillance, he was reading banned books, including What Is to Be Done? and other big questions about freedom and the individual. Anita's comment in the episode is: the surveillance here was not done well enough.

21:11 He gave himself the name of a bandit
On the banned list was a Georgian novel, Alexander Kazbegi's The Patricide, whose protagonist is a mountain outlaw named Koba. He took that name as his own alias, and at the seminary his classmates called him by it. The episode calls this a kind of "name determinism": he first took the name of a bandit hero, and then he really did become a bandit. The turning point from seminary student to bandit began when he saw with his own eyes two mountain bandits publicly hanged in the center of Gori for shooting a policeman over a stray cow — he was forbidden to watch, but he went.

24:16 They robbed 250,000 rubles and could not spend a single one
In 1907 he and a group of friends ambushed a bank carriage in Yerevan Square in Tiflis, almost within sight of the seminary: some stood on high ground throwing bombs down, others fired in the street, and the man organizing, financing and directing it all behind the scenes was Stalin, under the alias Koba. They got away with 250,000 rubles packed in linen sacks. But the bank had already published the serial numbers of its largest-denomination notes, so not one ruble of the money could be spent. It was the first time he left a police photograph on file, but he did not go to prison for it and essentially walked away untouched.

item.title: Outbound Reply Rates Near Zero? Don't Blame the Copy First — Check Who You're Sending To
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-ycsp-外联回复率接近零-先别怪文案-先查你在发给谁/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-ycsp-外联回复率接近零-先别怪文案-先查你在发给谁/
item.description: Outbound is like finding a needle in a haystack: get the person wrong and even perfect copy won't land. The YC partner's debugging order is — check the recipient first, then the company, then the subject line, and only then the copy.
item.content:encoded:
Outbound is like finding a needle in a haystack: get the person wrong and even perfect copy won't land. The YC partner's debugging order is — check the recipient first, then the company, then the subject line, and only then the copy.

Eight tactics in 12 minutes — dense, but every one is an action you can take immediately. For founders stuck at single-digit outbound reply rates who don't know what to change.

0:00 Send a hundred by hand before you talk about automation
The most common founder mistake is opening a tool, blasting a thousand emails, and getting zero replies. The real loss isn't the zero replies themselves — it's that you learned nothing from them. The problem could be the copy, the company targeting, the lead filtering, deliverability, or the subject line, and you can't tell which. So the advice is to do at least a hundred outbound attempts manually before automating, and genuinely manually: spend time researching one specific person, what her problem is, what would grab her attention, read her LinkedIn and her company page. That hands-on homework is where high-converting outbound ideas come from.

1:04 Picking the right person matters far more than polishing copy
Founders often spend hours tweaking email wording while barely thinking about who they're sending to. Outbound is like finding a needle in a haystack: you have to find the person who has exactly the pain point you solve, or the most carefully polished copy won't land. One winter batch company selling an infrastructure product should have been selling to senior engineering leaders, but its actual list was full of dev rel managers, GTM managers, and even customer success managers — hundreds of emails sent, and naturally no replies. Those wrong titles were never going to buy, regardless of how well the email was written.

2:06 Work backward from closed customers to the target title
How do you find the right title? Look at your existing customers first, then at the sales process: who pushed the last deal over the line, who signed the contract, who paid the money — list all their titles and go find people with similar profiles. You can also look at who has replied to your outbound. If you're still at the very earliest stage, with neither customers nor replies, ask yourself: who in the organization benefits most from buying your software. Example: selling employee device security monitoring software, the chief security officer could get fired in a data breach, so he'll be interested; an engineering manager would probably rather not be monitored, so he's not a good target.

3:09 List-building tools will hand you the wrong companies
Another common mistake is searching in Sales Navigator and getting back a pile of results that look like a match but are the wrong type of company — search tech companies, for instance, and you often get a bunch of IT implementation consultancies. So use list-building tools very carefully, and verify company by company whether they're really your customer. After doing enough outbound, you start noticing the clues that a company needs your product — intent signals. Job postings are a great observation point, since they reveal a company's priorities; company growth is another common signal: selling compensation planning software, companies under 100 people probably haven't introduced job levels yet, and companies over 500 have probably already set their comp bands, so crossing the 100-person mark is a great signal. Every product has signals like this; your job is to find your own.

4:09 Shake the tree of your personal network for your first customers
When closing your first few customers, starting from your personal network is much easier and converts at a much higher rate. Really shake the tree — make sure you've covered everyone you know: your personal network first, then ask friends, family, investors, college roommates, people you met at a coffee shop for intros — literally anyone you can think of.

5:10 Executives don't care about your product features
The single most important thing in the email is clearly stating how you can help the other person. Figure out the three things that keep the buyer up at night: what gets him fired, what gets him promoted, and why he should believe you can help. When a buyer reads the email and thinks "this is exactly my problem," they're likely willing to take the call, even if they don't yet fully understand or trust your solution. The fact is executives don't care about your product features, don't care that your upload speed is blazing fast, and don't care that your database is written in rust — what they worry about is hitting their quarterly targets. Keep the product description to one sentence at most, and save the details for the first call.

6:14 A good email reads like a peer wrote it, not like a pitch
The email from the founder of Aptin, a YC company in the S24 batch, is held up as an example: the tone is very casual, it sounds like a peer, it uses no jargon, it doesn't try to sound impressive, it reads like something a friend sent. He builds credibility with the first sentence — "I used to be a software engineer at Tesla. We got crazy good at using SMS to convert the people who visited our website into car buyers." The ending has a very clear call to action: would you be open to running an experiment to see whether AI can reactivate leads and lift conversion. The email also mentions that he noticed the phone number collected in the signup flow on their site, which makes it feel personalized; and it barely explains how the product works at all — it only talks about how to help the other person solve their problem.

8:20 On LinkedIn, mutual connections are the top predictor
If email is about the subject line, LinkedIn is about your profile — it determines whether people accept your connection request and whether they reply. Key points: a photo boosts trust; turn the top banner into an ad for your company, stating clearly and concisely what the company does, avoiding jargon; rewrite your one-line headline and about section into a short company description; move up what buyers care about (relevant and impressive experience, say) and cut what's irrelevant — if the about section is a pile of hobbies and interests, it's harder for a buyer to see how you can help him. Another place worth investing in is mutual connections: the number of shared connections is the single biggest predictor of whether someone accepts a connection request, so build up relevant mutual connections with your target audience — that takes time, and you should turn it into a habit of using your full connection quota every day.

item.title: World Models Are Not Video Generation: Atlas Makes 3D Control an Input
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-a16z-世界模型不是视频生成-atlas-把-3d-控制做成了输入/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-a16z-世界模型不是视频生成-atlas-把-3d-控制做成了输入/
item.description: Language models process tokens; world models process physical space. Atlas's key move is not generating longer video but putting the camera and reference images into 3D coordinates as inputs, turning generation from a slot machine into directing.
item.content:encoded:
Language models process tokens; world models process physical space. Atlas's key move is not generating longer video but putting the camera and reference images into 3D coordinates as inputs, turning generation from a slot machine into directing.

23 minutes, medium information density, but Justin draws the line between world models and video generation very clearly. Worth listening for anyone working in 3D, robotics, or VFX.

1:05 Atlas is a model release, not a product release
Justin clarifies right at the start: Atlas is not a product, it is World Labs's foundation model; products come later. It does three things — generate worlds that don't exist, reconstruct from real spaces, and simulate inside reconstructed spaces. Generation can start from text or an image, then you directly control the camera flying through that world; reconstruction can use just one photo, or a hundred or more, and the more photos the more accurate the reconstruction; simulation is aimed at VFX and robotics. This order itself shows World Labs does not intend to build a consumer app first, but to establish a horizontal foundation model first and let products grow on top of it.

4:09 Reference images are pinned in 3D space, not fed to the model
Video models tend to drift and hallucinate direction after about ten seconds. Justin says Atlas's solution is spatial context: the reference images you give are not ordinary images but are grounded in 3D space, and you can specify ‘put this one here, that one there’. When generating video you are not just giving a text prompt but directly controlling the camera, telling it to fly in this direction or that, achieving precise pixel-level control. So even when generating up to a minute, it is not pulling a slot machine — you are generating, directing, and controlling what the model outputs.

7:10 Atlas moves the 2D/3D fork earlier
Compared with World Labs's first product Marble, Atlas is a completely rebuilt model stack. Marble put Gaussian splat at the center; outputting video, 3D scenes, or mesh all had to go through a Gaussian representation first, then render back to image or video. Atlas breaks that dependency: the architecture is more unified and easier to scale, and the 2D/3D fork happens earlier. When generating 2D or video output, the bottleneck is no longer the Gaussian scene; the model directly produces 2D pixels. Only in applications where you actually need 3D does it lift to 3D.

8:10 Gaussian isn't obsolete, it's just no longer mandatory
Justin does not think Gaussian has been outgrown; it is just a tool, to be used in the right place. The final product of VFX is a 2D image or video, and may not need explicit 3D at all. But in real-time applications and embedded devices, explicit 3D representations like Gaussian and mesh still have a place: in the future you might stream pixels in real time from a server farm, but we are not there yet, and it would be expensive, so for client-side rendering, mobile, and VR devices, Gaussian or mesh remain useful. Another role is plugging into existing workflows — people in games, VFX, design, and architecture already have pipelines based on 3D representations, and rather than making them switch to fully AI-native all at once, it is better to let AI enter their workflows.

11:13 Simulation fills the last stretch of robot training
The value of real to sim for robots, Justin says, is first of all evaluation: a robot ultimately has to work in a specific factory, with specific machines, in a specific environment, and you need to make sure it works exactly there. So simulation is useful in the last stretch of training and evaluation — build a simulation as close as possible to the final use case, then either fine-tune a pretrained robot foundation model directly in that simulation, or run evaluations to confirm it works. This gives you a path different from ‘collect lots of demonstrations or human teleoperation’. He also describes a more radical version: take a few photos or casual videos with a phone, reconstruct the space with Atlas, describe the task in natural language, let an agent build the simulation and do RL fine-tuning, and within minutes you have a robot adapted to that space.

14:16 OpenAI dropping world models may be an innovator's dilemma
The host asks why OpenAI turned the Sora direction — ‘video generation models are world simulators’ — into a consumer product back then, and now doesn't do world models. Justin says he won't comment on OpenAI's internal strategy, but offers an explanation: there may be an innovator's dilemma — you hold something as strong as the LLM and lead in that direction, so investing in the next thing may not be worth it. World Labs's judgment is that there is another class of models here, with a lot of opportunity, and they want to be the ones to seize it.

18:21 Three iPhones produce bullet time, far better than expected
Asked about hard physics, Justin says he hasn't tried a black hole and guesses it wouldn't be too impressive. But what really surprised him was bullet time: using three iPhones on tripods for synchronized capture, then using Atlas to do a frozen-frame, orbit-around recomposition. He gives the official example — a strawberry dropping into oat milk, freezing time at the instant the milk splashes, flying around it in a circle, and the effect is completely insane. This capability needs only three input viewpoints. This shows Atlas's value is not only in ‘generating new worlds’ but also in turning a small amount of real footage into shots that traditionally required a large camera array.

19:21 3D is undervalued on the input side
Justin says 3D has value in two places. The output side has been much discussed — sometimes you just need explicit 3D assets to plug into a workflow or game engine. But the value of 3D on the input side is undervalued: even if the final output is a 2D VFX shot, letting the model provide a 3D control surface helps the director decide what kind of scene the model should output. You don't want to write ‘push in, pull out, move left’ in text; you want to grab the camera directly and make it zoom exactly the way you want — which text simply cannot describe. So Atlas makes camera control a native input type; one of the modalities in multimodality is the camera.

item.title: Making a furin site isn't hard at all — admitting it isn't rare is
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-twiv-造一个-furin-位点根本不难-难的是承认它不罕见/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-twiv-造一个-furin-位点根本不难-难的是承认它不罕见/
item.description: Deep sequencing shows that a few genomes in every thousand carry an insertion, and a furin site has been hit independently at the same position at least three times — the probabilistic argument for a lab origin doesn't hold up.
item.content:encoded:
Deep sequencing shows that a few genomes in every thousand carry an insertion, and a furin site has been hit independently at the same position at least three times — the probabilistic argument for a lab origin doesn't hold up.

The first half is the quantitative methodology of viral recombination and insertion; the second half is the real target of this episode: dismantling the lab-origin argument with numbers. Listeners who want the argument can jump straight to 52 minutes.

6:07 They changed the GFP sequence and the recombination rate went up
The team first built an OC43 reverse-genetics system and made a pair of viruses: each carries a frameshifted GFP, so infection alone yields only fragments, but coinfection lets recombination stitch green fluorescent protein back together. They expected that changing the nucleotide sequence of one of the GFPs would lower the recombination rate; instead it rose. Paul says there is only a hypothesis for this, no data — one possibility is that after double-stranded RNA forms, strand-transfer events during recombination become more likely because the duplex "breathes." This counterintuitive result later became the reagent starting point for the whole paper.

11:12 Knock GFP out of frame and let insertions reveal themselves
Measuring insertions and deletions is far harder than measuring point mutations, because they were thought to be rare and sequencing depth was insufficient. Their approach was to put the GFP gene into the viral genome and then deliberately knock it out of frame, preceded by a start-codon peptide that is in a different frame from GFP, so the virus does not glow green; it turns green only when that site acquires an insertion or deletion of a particular length that pulls GFP back into frame. This lets them both count event frequencies and pick out green viruses to sequence back and infer the mechanism. This is where figure 1 of the paper comes from.

13:15 Knocking out NSP15 made insertions go down, not up
The original hypothesis came from prior work suggesting that NSP15, a nuclease, affects deletion rates — think nuclease and you naturally think deletions, not insertions. But the experiment went the other way: viruses with NSP15 showed a greatly increased rate of acquiring insertions that pulled GFP back into frame. Paul says the deletion rate numbers were not good enough this time to quantify, but the insertion result was black and white, and they were very surprised — it was this accidental result that opened up the whole line of research.

22:26 Every base sequenced a million times before you talk frequency
They moved from picking green viruses to brute-force sequencing: concentrating about 10 milliliters of virus down to 1 milliliter, loading part of it onto a sequencing chip, and producing hundreds of millions of reads, so that every nucleotide in the genome is read at least a million times, with roughly 30 human genomes' or 3 million viral genomes' worth of data per virus stock. Paul stresses that depth has to match the number of virions in the sample — sequencing hundreds of millions of times when the tube holds only a thousand virions is meaningless; they calibrated to sequence roughly a few percent of the virions in the sample.

27:32 Eleven nucleotides is the threshold for judging origin
Short insertions (three to six nucleotides) can arise randomly in a viral genome, so their origin cannot be determined, and they were excluded from the analysis. They calculated that if an 11-nucleotide stretch perfectly matches the viral genome, the probability of that being pure chance is below 5%, so they restricted the analysis to insertions of 11 nucleotides or more. The result: over 90% matched the viral genome perfectly or nearly perfectly, and in OC43 wild-type virus had 87 times more insertions than the NSP15 mutant, most of them derived from the positive strand.

36:41 Insertions aren't rare events — they're a few per thousand
Vincent says he was told for years that insertions are rare, but the data suggest this is happening all the time. Paul responds that "rare" is a relative term: one in a million is rare, but if you have ten million of them, it's common. The insertion frequency they report is a few genomes per thousand — roughly five to ten genomes carrying an insertion per thousand virions. That is lower than the point-mutation rate, but not by much. The reason it seemed rare in the past is that the vast majority of insertions are harmful or even lethal to the virus and get purged at low multiplicity of infection, so you never isolate them.

55:05 Making a furin site isn't hard at all
Mechanistically, a furin cleavage site needs at minimum two arginines, RXXR, and can even be cleaved with a single arginine plus other amino acids in the right places. Six of the 64 codons encode arginine, so multiplying the two fractions, about 1% of random 12-base sequences encode an RXR motif. The coronavirus genome has roughly 30,000 different positions where an insertion mutation can occur. So this is not some enormous engineering challenge.

57:08 Lightning strikes the same spot at least three times
Putting the insertion frequency, the number of insertable sites, and the viral population size together, the probability of a furin cleavage site appearing at one particular position in a coronavirus genome is not astonishing, and it roughly matches what deep sequencing actually measures. In their deep-sequencing data, which does not cover the whole population, they have already found new furin cleavage sites independently at least three times at the exact position of SARS-CoV-2's existing furin site. Paul says the numbers in the paper are an underestimate: they only focused on the spike region for PCR, and they required insertions to match the viral genome perfectly to rule out PCR artifacts, which very likely also excluded some real natural sites.

item.title: Rome Won With a Crow: The Key to the First Punic War
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-ancients-罗马的胜利靠一只乌鸦-第一次布匿战争的关键/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-ancients-罗马的胜利靠一只乌鸦-第一次布匿战争的关键/
item.description: Rome turned sea battles into land battles with a boarding bridge called the corvus, cancelling Carthage's advantage in seamanship; but Carthage brought in a Spartan to rebuild its army and captured a Roman consul in return.
item.content:encoded:
Rome turned sea battles into land battles with a boarding bridge called the corvus, cancelling Carthage's advantage in seamanship; but Carthage brought in a Spartan to rebuild its army and captured a Roman consul in return.

This episode tells the First Punic War as a war story with mechanisms: the crow bridge, the sacred chickens, mercenaries, war elephants — all backed by concrete images and numbers, at high information density.

2:03 This was not a war between two equal powers
The host opens by calling this a clash of ‘the two great powers of the western Mediterranean,’ and Eve MacDonald corrects him on the spot: at the war's outbreak, Carthage was not necessarily a military power of that rank. Carthage had money, controlled the sea routes, and had centuries of alliance networks in western Sicily, but it had no strong standing army — it relied on allies and mercenaries. What actually made Carthage into a power capable of fighting Rome as an equal was this war itself.
