So the story Roman sources tell over and over, of ‘Roman adaptability,’ is only half the story; the other half is Carthaginian resilience and adaptability, without which there is no explaining why this war lasted more than twenty years.

15:29 Mercenaries at Messana dragged both powers into war
The trigger was not the ambition of Rome or Carthage but a group of Campanian mercenaries called the Mamertines. They had seized Messana, and after being defeated by Hiero II, king of Syracuse, they split in two: one faction asked Carthage for help, the other asked Rome. Carthage acted first from its base in the Lipari Islands, and Rome followed — and not with a small intervention, but a full invasion with two consular armies. Eve points out that the Roman sources' claim of an ‘accidental empire’ is highly suspect, because the Romans showed up at Messana at the scale of an invading force. Polybius treats the Romans' first crossing of the sea into Sicily as the starting point of Roman imperial expansion.

28:14 The corvus turned sea battles into land battles
Carthage was a naval power, with skilled oarsmen and ships built fast and well — the Romans even built their warships to Carthaginian standards. But the Romans added one thing: the corvus, meaning ‘crow,’ a boarding bridge that could hook an enemy ship. Once hooked, the Carthaginian ship could not move, and Roman marines simply crossed over and fought a land battle. At the Battle of Mylae, the Carthaginians clearly had not expected this, and suffered heavy losses. Eve also cautions that the details of the corvus leave many unanswerable questions in the sources, but ancient historians all treat it as decisive. At the Battle of Cape Ecnomus, the corvus was again credited as the chief factor, and Rome thereby opened the sea route for its invasion of Africa.

38:40 Carthage hired a Spartan to rebuild its army
After the Roman landing in Africa, Rome advanced steadily and Carthage looked finished. Carthage's response was to recruit a new army in the eastern Mediterranean and bring in a Spartan commander, Xanthippus. He reorganised the Carthaginian army and reworked how the war elephants were used. Eve notes in particular that the Carthaginians had not used war elephants before; it was only after seeing the Indian elephants Pyrrhus brought that they realised they had a smaller African elephant of their own they could use. Xanthippus's reforms worked: the Roman army was destroyed and the consul Regulus was captured. This was Rome's first devastating defeat of the war, and it became a key event in later Roman memory defining the relationship between Rome and Carthage.

43:11 The captured consul went back to Rome to argue against peace
Carthage sent the captured consul Regulus back to Rome to negotiate peace. In the Senate, Regulus said not to surrender, that Carthage was there for the taking. By agreement, if peace failed he had to return to Carthage and remain a prisoner. He went back, and died in captivity. Eve says the various horrific versions of how he died are not actually mentioned in the credible sources, so it is hard to judge how much is later embellishment; but what is certain is that he died in captivity in Carthage, peace was refused, and Rome fought on. This passage is a classic moment of Roman self-congratulatory rhetoric.

46:27 The sacred chickens would not eat, and the Roman fleet was finished
In 249 BC, the Roman consul Tiberius Claudius Pulcher led a fleet against Carthage off Drepana. By Roman ritual, the sacred chickens on his ship had to eat for battle to be joined, otherwise it was a bad omen. The chickens would not eat, so he threw them into the sea, saying that if they would not eat, they could drink. Roman sources present this as the most serious act of sacrilege, and the Roman fleet was then defeated at Drepana. Eve says that once Roman sources start emphasising a commander's arrogance and contempt for tradition, it usually means something bad happened. This defeat kept Rome from sending out a fleet for eight years.

50:48 Hannibal's father held Rome down with guerrilla war
After Drepana, Rome vanished from the sea and Carthage gained freedom of action on the western coast. In 247 BC, Carthage sent a new commander, Hamilcar Barca — Hannibal's father. He brought a force Polybius calls the Mix-Hellenes, made up of soldiers of Greek, Libyan and Phoenician descent from North Africa, and waged guerrilla war against Rome, occupying high ground above Drepana and Panormus with considerable success. Eve says this was the first time in the war that the Carthaginian army fought Rome this well. He also seized the temple complex at Eryx, dedicated to the goddess the Carthaginians called Astarte, and both sides fought fiercely over this sacred site.

57:20 The rams from this war still lie on the seabed
The Battle of the Aegates Islands in 241 BC was the last battle. The Roman fleet hid behind the islands and ambushed a Carthaginian fleet loaded with supplies meant for Hamilcar. Eve says that if you climb Eryx today, on a clear day you can see the Aegates Islands perfectly, and Hamilcar very likely watched this disaster unfold from land. More remarkably, the site of this sea battle has been preserved underwater: over the past twenty years, underwater archaeologists have found large bronze rams on the seabed near the island of Levanzo, some inscribed with the names of Roman consuls, some bearing Punic inscriptions and carvings, along with Monte Fortino helmets and amphorae.

item.title: Bunsen Burners Don't Reduce Plate Contamination, and Vegetables Protect the Heart by Another Mechanism
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-thisweekinmicr-本生灯不减少平板污染-蔬菜护心另有机制/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-thisweekinmicr-本生灯不减少平板污染-蔬菜护心另有机制/
item.description: A Bunsen burner may actually increase settle colonies in low-contamination environments; the cardiovascular benefit of vegetables may not run through the nitrate-nitrite-NO pathway but through gut bacteria turning nitrate and iron into DNIC that directly activates sGC.
item.content:encoded:
A Bunsen burner may actually increase settle colonies in low-contamination environments; the cardiovascular benefit of vegetables may not run through the nitrate-nitrite-NO pathway but through gut bacteria turning nitrate and iron into DNIC that directly activates sGC.

The first half has clean experimental design and a counterintuitive conclusion; the second half's DNIC paper has a complete mechanism but dense terminology, suited to those willing to chew through mechanism.

6:05 Bunsen burners don't reduce plate contamination
The authors used paired settle plates: one placed next to a lit Bunsen burner, one next to an unlit burner, both exposed simultaneously to the same contamination airflow. The lit burner overall did not lower average contamination, and the statistical comparison showed no significant improvement. This directly challenges the common claim that there is a general sterile halo around the blue flame. The authors don't say the burner never helps, but that the effect depends on environmental conditions — they deliberately contaminated the lab air with Gordonia rubripertincta, then compared different flame sizes and dry versus wet particles.

10:13 83 CFU per minute is the crossover point
Under dry-particle conditions with an average 18 mm flame, they observed an apparent crossover point: when airborne microbial concentration was above 83 CFU/minute, settle on plates next to the burner tended to decrease; below that level, settle tended to increase instead. This can explain decades of contradictory anecdotal experience: people in dry environments genuinely believe the burner helps, while people in modern air-conditioned labs with low airborne contamination genuinely find it useless or even worse. Relative humidity in a typical modern air-conditioned lab is usually between 40% and 60%.

13:43 Airflow isn't one-dimensional — don't light a burner in a laminar flow hood
Convention holds that convection pulls contaminants upward, but the authors point out that the same airflow may first drag contaminated air laterally across the work surface before it rises. Any upward airflow must draw replacement air from somewhere, so the most important thing during aseptic work is to limit wind or airflow. This leads to the most practical point in the episode: there is no reason to light a Bunsen burner in a laminar flow hood, since the flame itself disrupts laminar flow. The authors did not directly visualize airflow — they measured a biologically relevant outcome, contamination, rather than directly measuring fluid dynamics, and the authors themselves list this as a limitation.

17:49 Flaming tube mouths and lighting burners are both ritual
The authors draw a historical comparison with the old practice of flaming culture tube mouths. Michael's graduate advisor at the time said stop doing it, there's no evidence it helps, and produced the 1972 paper proving it. The judgment in the episode is: changing behavior is hard, especially when a ritual gives people a sense of control — lighting the burner feels proactive, flaming the tube mouth feels like protecting the culture, but there's no evidence it actually does anything. The authors don't argue for abandoning the Bunsen burner; they argue for measuring: use simple settle plates to measure your own lab's environment and let evidence guide practice.

28:14 Vegetables may protect the heart via the DNIC pathway
This Cell paper proposes reframing the entire nitric oxide synthase pathway: not a local paracrine model (eNOS makes NO acting on adjacent smooth muscle), but an endocrine-like circuit — nitric oxide synthase makes nitrate, nitrate enters the gut, is turned by microbes into dinitrosyl iron compounds (DNIC), which then act on targets such as the heart. If it holds, the cardiovascular benefit of dietary nitrate (leafy greens, beets) may be mainly mediated by microbe-generated DNIC, rather than the nitrate-nitrite-NO pathway we currently believe in. The author is Andrei Kleshioff at the Karolinska Institute.

31:32 No DNIC found in germ-free mice
They used electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) to directly detect DNIC in tissues. Signals were visible in the liver and kidney of healthy mice, but running the same assay on germ-free mice found no DNIC at all in the tissue — the first hint that microbes are making it. After feeding inorganic nitrate, liver DNIC levels rose in conventional mice but not in germ-free mice; if ferric citrate was added to the nitrate drinking water, the liver DNIC signal rose even higher, while ferric citrate alone had no effect. Same in vitro: mouse and human feces plus nitrate plus iron can make DNIC, while germ-free mouse feces cannot.

39:55 DNIC directly activates sGC, not via free NO
They used isolated mouse aortic rings, first pre-contracted with phenylephrine, then added DNIC. To distinguish free NO from direct sGC activation, they used two pharmacological tools: one scavenging free NO, one directly blocking sGC. The sGC blocker completely abolished DNIC-induced relaxation, while the free-NO scavenger only partially attenuated it. The conclusion is that DNIC activates sGC, but not through free NO — the FeNO2 entity itself appears to directly activate sGC. The same holds for bacteria-generated DNIC: only wild-type E. coli supernatant (anaerobic, with nitrate and iron) relaxed aortic rings, while a nitrate reductase-deficient mutant did not.

47:16 DNIC suppresses leucine uptake, holding down mTORC1
On the metabolic line, they measured the phosphorylation state of key proteins in the liver mTORC1 pathway. In disease-model mice mTORC1 was overactivated, downstream S6K1 phosphorylation was elevated, and transcription factors driving lipid synthesis were also elevated. Both DNIC treatment and nitrate-plus-iron supplementation brought these markers back to control levels. Mechanistically, they used glioblastoma cells to measure radiolabeled leucine uptake and found DNIC inhibits leucine uptake in a concentration-dependent manner, suggesting it inhibits the leucine transporter — leucine is the key signal telling mTORC1 that nutrients are available, so blocking uptake blocks mTORC1 activation.

item.title: Private credit's risk hides in insurance company ratings
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-excessreturns-私募信贷的风险藏在保险公司的评级里/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-excessreturns-私募信贷的风险藏在保险公司的评级里/
item.description: Private credit has poured into insurance companies, much of it in affiliated investments, rated by private agencies that are systematically too generous; on correct ratings, insurers would have to hold an extra $400-500 billion of capital a year.
item.content:encoded:
Private credit has poured into insurance companies, much of it in affiliated investments, rated by private agencies that are systematically too generous; on correct ratings, insurers would have to hold an extra $400-500 billion of capital a year.

The first half is industry anecdote; the specific mechanisms and numbers in the middle and back half — private credit ratings, private equity in 401ks, Social Security reform — are the part that is actually worth money.

5:08 A stock fund should be 80-90% stocks
When Bob Posen took over as president of Fidelity in 1995, the firm was in an awkward spot: Jeff Vinick had moved half of the Magellan fund into cash, which both dragged on performance and violated holders' expectations of a stock fund. His approach was to build consensus internally first — if the fund you run is a stock fund, you have to keep 80% to 90% of the position in the kind of stocks the fund's name implies; if you want balanced, if you want a money market fund, the firm has other products. His logic: investors bought this fund's positioning, and a manager cannot change that positioning just because he thinks ‘now is not a good time to buy stocks’. That rule later became basic discipline for Fidelity's stock funds.

8:12 After doubling in size, keep the startup feel by splitting into small teams
Under Posen, Fidelity's assets under management grew from $500 billion to $1 trillion. His judgment was that the key to managing that much money is not process but how to preserve entrepreneurial spirit and a sense of belonging. The method was to split the investment team into relatively small groups — value, growth, small cap, international and so on — so each group had a stronger sense of ownership over results. At the same time he consolidated money market and bond funds into New Hampshire, because fixed income and money market funds look at the same credits, and here scale is a friend that spreads out enormous economies of scale; stock funds are exactly the opposite.

19:21 Put private equity in 401ks, but cap it at 10-20% first
Posen is reserved about putting private equity into 401ks. The core problem is liquidity: if a participant puts all of their retirement assets into a single private equity fund, when a medical emergency hits or they reach the age for required minimum distributions, they simply cannot get the money out. His proposal is that private equity can only be part of an asset allocation fund or a target date fund, not a standalone option; if it must be a standalone option, employers should set a cap, and the magnitude he gives is 10% to 20%. He draws an analogy to employer stock: GE employees who put their whole 401k into GE stock did not end up well, and a retirement account needs diversification.

21:25 The instant markup in secondary trades is an accounting loophole
Private equity is hard to value to begin with, and what worries Posen most is secondary trading: a private fund, because it needs to raise cash or its investment period is ending, sells part of its portfolio at a discount to another private fund. There is a technical loophole in the accounting rules that lets the buyer, even having bought at a 5% discount, immediately mark that investment up to face value on the books. He thinks this rule has to change. Valuation is already hard enough; this kind of ‘instant markup’ should not be allowed to lift book value out of thin air and pass it through NAV to holders.

24:28 Private ratings systematically overstate private credit
The private credit held by insurance companies, depending on how you count, can be as much as $2 trillion, and a large part of it is ‘affiliated investment’ — starting with Apollo, more and more private equity firms have become owners of insurance companies and then put debt related to themselves into their own insurers. Posen and his co-authors found that a great deal of private credit is rated by private rating agencies, and that rating shopping exists. Two studies, from Columbia and Imperial College, show these private ratings are systematically too high; on correct ratings, insurers would have to hold an extra $400 billion to $500 billion of capital a year. His solution is direct: make the private ratings public and let the market pick apart the assumptions and methodology.

29:35 Mark Walter's $20 billion of affiliated credit is a wake-up call
Posen treats the Mark Walter case as a wake-up call. Walter founded Guggenheim and figured out early that buying a life insurer lets you steer what was a conservative insurance portfolio into higher-yielding securities, including private credit related to Guggenheim or to your own portfolio companies. The rules themselves allow insurers to invest in affiliated private credit, provided it is disclosed to regulators. Regulators have now found that insurers controlled by Walter or Guggenheim hold about $20 billion of affiliated private credit, some of which may have been used to buy the Los Angeles Dodgers and the Lakers. Walter's side is trying to divest part of the affiliated credit. Posen stresses this is not just Guggenheim: large private funds such as Apollo and KKR have all found insurance companies to be useful investment vehicles.

41:52 Someone with $1 million of investable assets should not hold 40% bonds
Posen points out that most target date funds arrive at retirement at 80% bonds and cash, 20% stocks, which is reasonable for someone who has to live off the retirement portfolio. But more than 7 million people in the US have investable assets (excluding their primary home) of over $1 million, they do not live off investment income, and they can withstand a down year in stocks. He calculates that over a 30-year horizon, a 60/40 portfolio and the 90/10 he advocates (90% stocks, 10% cash) differ by a factor of two in terminal value, the equivalent of $5 million versus $2.5 million. He rebuts the objections one by one: over the past 60 years bonds only acted as a hedge in 10 of them; in 2022 stocks and bonds both fell about 18%; stocks fall deeply, but look at two years, five years — after 2008, 2002 and 1974 they all recovered and went higher.

50:09 Semiannual reports are fine, but don't scrap first- and third-quarter filings
Posen supports keeping quarterly reporting and opposes moving to semiannual. The reason is that the economy, diplomacy and a company's own situation all change quickly, and six months is a long time; and the information vacuum created by semiannual reporting encourages insider trading. His compromise: at mid-year and year-end, file full 10-Qs and 10-Ks; in the first and third quarters, file a slimmed-down report, three or four pages plus the income statement and balance sheet, which is not a big burden. He rebuts the claim that ‘less reporting encourages long-termism’: when the UK made the move from quarterly to semiannual reporting optional in 2013-14, he and a quantitative accounting scholar at Columbia compared the two groups of companies, and the companies that switched to semiannual did not invest more in R&D or capital expenditure.

item.title: Astra Crosses the AGI Threshold, but No One Can Audit It
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-cogrev-astra-跨过-agi-门槛-但没人能审计它/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-cogrev-astra-跨过-agi-门槛-但没人能审计它/
item.description: Astra frees humans from ever having to do certain tasks again, yet OpenAI paused only half its RL compute; external audits get stuck two or three days before release, and there is no adult in the room to take the blame.
item.content:encoded:
Astra frees humans from ever having to do certain tasks again, yet OpenAI paused only half its RL compute; external audits get stuck two or three days before release, and there is no adult in the room to take the blame.

The two hosts chain together Astra's capability evidence, the true magnitude of OpenAI's pause announcement, why audits can't get off the ground, and why doomers can't hedge their bets — high information density.

3:30 Astra holds long tasks together with a single notes file
In the past, models handling long tasks compressed a million tokens into a summary and opened a new window, losing all the detail. Astra instead maintains a long-lived notes file that the model updates at any time, moving forward with it no matter how many tokens have already been written, and it can also search back through its own session history. So the same million-token context window can effectively manage roughly ten times that much context within a single rollout. Nathan calls this a mechanism that is "obvious in hindsight, but genuinely new."

6:19 OpenAI self-reports 3.1 agent workdays per workday
In its research-acceleration blog post, OpenAI gives its own unit of measure, the "agent workday," reporting that each human workday corresponds to 3.1 agent workdays. Nathan admits the methodology is unclear; his reading is the literal one: for every eight-hour shift a human researcher puts in, the agent runs twenty-four hours in real time. The same post also has a chart grouping by human time spent and looking at Astra's success rate, effectively a substitute for the METR curve. Nathan says the METR curve hasn't been updated in a long time — not for lack of wanting to, but because the tasks aren't big enough anymore: the model iteration cycle is now shorter than the task length that needs to be measured.

21:03 External audits are structurally stuck at two or three days
Prakash breaks down why external audits can't get off the ground: there are a hundred candidates in a model's lifecycle, and the release version is only settled in the final two or three days, so external auditors get only a few days. Bringing the audit team into the company a month early runs into a second layer of problems — audit firms are short on people and money, depend on model-company funding, and their staff keep flowing to model companies; and if two companies agreed not to poach from audit firms, that would itself be an antitrust problem. He says the revolving-door problem in financial-industry regulation remains unsolved to this day.

31:12 What was announced as a pause actually stopped only half
Nathan reads OpenAI's RL compute chart: what was announced was a "frontier scale RL pause," but in reality, when the Hugging Face incident was disclosed, half was stopped first and the other half kept running — and that half was already enough for the Astra model to take over part of OpenAI's research infrastructure; even so, it wasn't fully stopped, only half was cut. As for whether the remaining blue compute labeled "non Astra" contains a model stronger than Astra, he says he doesn't know, but "I've been disappointed before." Prakash adds: the real frontier model isn't the one deployed, nor the one being trained, but the one in the researcher's head, because those ideas become models twelve to eighteen months later.

39:05 There is no adult in the room to take the blame
Prakash's rebuttal to Jacob Coxen's line that "accepting this race and entering the endgame is an arrogant gamble launched from a private company's Slack" is: then who do you want to hand it to? Pete Hegseth's Signal group? His judgment is that there is "no adult in the room" — no external savior, the whole world is held together with tape, and most of the smartest, most capable people to handle this are already inside these companies. Hand the decision to the government and what you get is political legitimacy, not wisdom, nor the legitimacy needed for execution. So the starting point must be accepting that the world is just like this.

46:03 Operation Warp Speed is the precedent for a safe harbor
Nathan proposes the government should set a hard deadline the way you would with a child: you sort it out yourselves, here's the deadline, and if you can't, I'll come in and be the bad guy. The accompanying move is to first remove the antitrust excuse. Prakash counters with Operation Warp Speed: the pharma companies specifically demanded immunity from vaccine claims, wanted a safe harbor, and actually got legislation; without that exemption, they would have been sued into bankruptcy after the pandemic. So lawyers warning that "there will be retroactive reckoning in the future" is not alarmism — even if all current decision-makers agree, it doesn't matter, because the only thing constraining future decision-makers is law, not the verbal promises of today's people.

1:00:40 FSD's mistake is putting a human in the loop
Raffi has crashed a Tesla using FSD. His judgment is that FSD's interface design is bad, because it claims a human in the loop but, when it hands control back to the user, doesn't give enough time to understand the situation and decide what to do; Waymo's design premise is that there is no human to take over, so the safety argument is entirely different. He personally would be willing to drive FSD again on the highway, or at least sit behind the wheel, but would hesitate on local streets in Palo Alto. The same company also has two kinds of code contracts: the Firefox team allows only humans to commit, while the Mozilla AI team has an entire codebase not a single human has written a line of — people only write specs, and the whole codebase is automatically regenerated at CI build time.

1:29:15 The takeover is already complete, no one just admits it
The key disagreement between Prakash and Daniel: Daniel hasn't realized this has already happened. The financial market itself is the paper clipper, the means of production is the financial market, and the financial market has already fully merged with AI. Humanity took about a hundred years to hand complete control of the means of production to the financial market. He says don't think of AI as a chat box; it's a global information process that doesn't have to run in a single box, and doesn't even have to be silicon-based — humans together with AI agents can constitute this information process. The reason Jacob became disillusioned is that he discovered in the Slack group that there was no control at all, yet he still assumed there existed somewhere in the world a group that could actually make decisions.

item.title: Enterprises will run 80% of tokens through open models, but spend only 20% of budget
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-ycsp-企业最终八成-token-走开源模型-但只花两成预算/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-ycsp-企业最终八成-token-走开源模型-但只花两成预算/
item.description: Open models and closed frontier models are not substitutes: the vast majority of tokens will go through open models, the hardest work stays with the frontier labs, and routing and orchestration connect the two in between.
item.content:encoded:
Open models and closed frontier models are not substitutes: the vast majority of tokens will go through open models, the hardest work stays with the frontier labs, and routing and orchestration connect the two in between.

The Ollama CEO gives first-hand token-flow data: local and cloud model mixes look nothing alike, and the real constraint on enterprise purchasing is security, not cost.

1:03 The driver behind open models is control, not saving money
Jeff says cost is the biggest pain point open models can solve immediately, but the enterprise north star is "better control over AI and customizing it for yourself." Cost is just the piece that can be solved in the short term; only once that is unlocked does customizing the model to your own use case come next. The order matters: if you treat open models purely as a cost-cutting lever, you will misjudge why they are spreading so fast inside the Fortune 500. AT&T has already moved 40% of its token consumption onto open models, currently mostly US and European models, while also evaluating Chinese ones.

4:05 Two inflection points: coding agents, then OpenClaw
The per-user token usage curve on Ollama's cloud has two clear inflection points. The first came early in the year, driven by coding agents — Kimi, GLM and MiniMax launched in succession, and for the first time open models could carry a coding agent. The second came in April, brought by OpenClaw, as users expanded from developers to non-developers: finance, customer service, marketing and sales can all hand a hard problem to an open model and let it run to completion, picking tools and pulling data along the way, burning enormous numbers of tokens. Context windows growing from 128K to over a million is the technical precondition for this burst.

8:08 Model launch day is a 24-hour fire drill
Ollama is a coordination channel for model vendors ahead of launches, but Jeff says getting a model weeks early counts as lucky; most of the work gets crammed into the final 24 hours before launch. Three things have to land at once: inference engine support (often weeks of work, to make sure it is fast, accurate and consistent with the reference implementation), the accompanying harness (there are plenty of open-source harnesses now, like Codex and OpenCode), and capacity from hardware and inference providers — launch day is usually the biggest growth day. He compares it to an operating system: drivers, inference layer and application runtime all have to be glued together, and it is a combinatorial explosion problem.

14:11 Above the token is where the new scarcity lives
Jeff cites three directions from Anthropic's platform team: knowledge (wiring company data and context into the model), coordination (one request spawns a pile of sub-agents, some in the cloud and some local, that need scheduling), and execution (sandboxes and compute). His judgment: tokens are already in oversupply, dozens of open model providers can supply them, and what is scarce is how to orchestrate an agent from A to B on top of those tokens. Following the path of cloud computing, developers ultimately prefer the best standalone product at every layer rather than something packaged together like Heroku or Google App Engine.

17:14 Stateful things will not sink into the model layer
Asked whether harnesses will be absorbed by models, Jeff's judgment is that the core loop and hooks will sink into the model, but a few categories cannot. One is state — models are trained on a monthly cadence and can never catch up with the latest data, so storage is a huge standalone problem space. The other is credential management and security. Open models do not come with a whole security toolkit the way closed providers do, and that is critical to enterprise adoption. This explains why the stronger the models get, the more middle layers there are.

18:15 80% of tokens run on open models, but only 20% of budget
Jeff's steady-state judgment: the vast majority of tokens inside an enterprise — his figure is 80% to 90% — will run on open models, but that does not mean 80% to 90% of budget goes to open source. The open community is driving costs extremely low, so maybe only 10% to 20% of spending lands on open models. The hardest work goes to the frontier labs, because that is where the best researchers are; the big middle is open and closed combined. He uses a law firm analogy: the partner hands work down to a pile of associates.

22:19 Local and cloud model mixes are not the same thing at all
On local models, US and Chinese models are roughly neck and neck; on cloud-hosted models, it is almost entirely Chinese models. Jeff says local is a three-way mix of US, European and Chinese, while cloud coding agents are dominated by Chinese models. The division of use cases is clear too: coding agents write code and tests, face many hard problems, and rely mainly on large cloud models; workflows with low end-to-end difficulty like document processing run very well locally. So it is a hybrid execution model — simple tasks run locally, plus a router deciding when to escalate to a large model.

29:25 The Flash tier is the precondition for unlimited tokens
Jeff says that early in the year open models had just caught up to the intelligence frontier, within less than 3 months of the closed frontier, and the next problem to solve is extreme efficiency. The key metric for models like DeepSeek Flash is not just low cost per token but low cost per task. These models are good enough for 80% of tasks, fast and extremely cheap, and will become the workhorse doing the grunt work. He recalls that in the ChatGPT era nobody thought about token usage, and we will eventually return to that state, but it requires model architectures trained specifically for high token volumes. The fastest-growing segment on Ollama's cloud is precisely the DeepSeek line, driven mainly by Flash adoption.

item.title: One Report Closed Over a Hundred Medical Schools, and Black Doctors Were Cut Off for a Generation
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-stuffmissed-一份报告关掉上百所医学院-黑人医生从此断层/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-stuffmissed-一份报告关掉上百所医学院-黑人医生从此断层/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: The Flexner Report is usually written up as the starting point of modern medical education, but it also closed five of seven Black medical schools, and for nearly forty years afterward no new Black medical school appeared.
item.content:encoded:
The Flexner Report is usually written up as the starting point of modern medical education, but it also closed five of seven Black medical schools, and for nearly forty years afterward no new Black medical school appeared.

Medium information density. The first half is a chronological slog through Flexner's life; the real value is in the second half, on how the report reshaped medical education and how it cut off the supply of Black doctors.

6:09 The report's author was not a doctor but an education reformer
Abraham Flexner was not a medical man. In 1890 he ran an experimental school with no fixed curriculum, no exams and no grades, and its students still got into good schools; in 1908 he wrote The American College, A Criticism, attacking American higher education, which is why Henry Smith Pritchett of the Carnegie Foundation came to him and asked him to turn the same critical eye on the medical schools of the United States and Canada. He spent two years travelling to 155 medical schools, recording admissions requirements, faculty, finances, laboratories and hospital affiliations school by school, and in 1910 delivered Medical Education in the United States and Canada. It was precisely because he was an outsider rather than a member of the medical community that the assessment dared to be so unsparing.

14:23 Medical schools were still teaching out-of-date knowledge
In the fifty years before the report, bacteriology, diagnostic technique and surgery were all changing fast, but medical schools had no common standards. At many schools the faculty were practising physicians who taught the way they themselves had been taught and did not update the content. The result was that the care the doctors they produced gave their patients was, at best, antiquated and, at worst, life-threatening. Admissions standards were just as chaotic: when the report was published, 74% of medical schools required only a high school diploma, some accepted even a high school equivalency certificate, only one in five required more than two years of college coursework, and many schools were essentially for-profit businesses.

18:31 He recommended closing 120 of the 155 schools
Flexner set standards first and then graded school by school: admission should require college-level biology, chemistry and physics; the curriculum should include classroom and laboratory work in anatomy, pathology, bacteriology and pharmacology; there should be a teaching hospital for hands-on practice; and teachers should be salaried, full-time teaching and research staff rather than physicians practising on the side. He published the results by state and by school, naming dirty laboratories and lax standards, and criticising course schedules that left students sitting for hours, exhausted, listening to dull lectures by part-time instructors. In the end he recommended closing 120 of the 155 schools. Within ten years the number of American medical schools was down to half, the surviving schools reformed their standards and curricula, and laboratory and clinical teaching were modernised on a large scale. In Canada only one school made the closure recommendation list, and in the end it did not close.

23:43 He never did the books on Black medical schools
The report was equally unsparing toward Black medical schools, writing that five of the seven "can make no valuable contribution at this moment", and affirming only Howard and Meharry as worth developing. But the assessment did not take into account that Black medical schools charged far lower tuition than white schools, had smaller endowments, and were already running on extremely thin margins. He wrote that "the Negro needs good schools rather than many schools", and said that one of the most important duties of Black doctors and Black nurses was to teach hygiene rather than life-saving skills — a statement that is itself racist. Every Black medical school he named as inadequate closed: the first four closed before 1914, the fifth in 1915, and the last held on until 1923.

25:48 The next Black medical school had to wait until 1966
Howard and Meharry survived and are still there today. But the next medical school aimed primarily at Black students was Charles R. Drew Medical School in Los Angeles, which did not open until 1966, and then in response to the health-access needs of the Black community; the one after that was Morehouse School of Medicine in Atlanta in 1975. The direct consequence of narrowing the options was a huge care gap: many potential doctors were shut out of educational opportunity by geography, and Black patients were often cared for by white doctors who, even at best, carried built-in racial bias. An expert panel convened by the AMA's Institute for Ethics in 2005 concluded that Flexner's "good schools rather than many schools" ensured that medicine remained segregated, and that the communities that most needed doctors were the ones left without them.

26:51 The AMA was paying behind Carnegie's project
One fact not disclosed at the time: the Carnegie Foundation hired Flexner for this project, and the AMA was also a sponsor. There is also an unresolved question — whether someone connected to the AMA accompanied him on some of the school visits. He said different things at different times, sometimes that the person went with him, later that they merely met there, so whether the report was subject to more direct directional influence cannot be determined to this day.

28:53 Did he know he was constraining Black medicine?
He knew. The report contains a passage of idealistic colouring, saying that building up Howard and Meharry would benefit the nation far more than barely sustaining more schools. In 1933 he wrote to the board of the institute he had founded, arguing that hiring and admissions must "not directly or indirectly consider race, religion or sex". One explanation comes from his biographer Thomas Neville Bonner: when Flexner was growing up in Louisville, the local Black community had more services and opportunities than in many places, with a dozen or so Black schools and vocational training in medicine and law for Black students; the Flexners were not well off, there were Black families among the neighbours, and he and his siblings often played with Black children in the community. This may have left him overly idealistic about the reality of Black family life, and he later admitted that it was not until he began studying educational institutions that he realised how disadvantaged those Black classmates of his had been.

35:01 The hygiene line may not have been his own
The claim that hygiene was the main duty of Black doctors is one of the key pieces of evidence for calling Flexner racist. But the leaders of Meharry and Howard had said similar things in 1907 and 1908 — two or three years before the report — and those leaders were white too. This suggests Flexner's formulation may have been a restatement of the schools' established mission rather than a judgement he arrived at independently. In 2011 Lynn E. Miller and Richard M. Weiss, writing in the Journal of the History of Medicine and Allied Sciences, proposed another possibility: that this language was in fact opening up a public health role for the doctors at these schools, in order to win support across the racial divide — because those statements about hygiene being the most urgent need were immediately followed by the conclusion that these institutions obviously ought to be supported. In 2008 the AMA issued a public apology for its history of racial inequality.

item.title: Change One Law of Physics and Every Wish Backfires
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-skeptics-改一条物理定律-每个愿望都会反噬/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-skeptics-改一条物理定律-每个愿望都会反噬/
item.category: The Skeptics' Guide to the Universe
item.description: A live thought experiment from Dragon Con: you may change exactly one law of physics to make science fiction real, and every wish gets taken apart for the consequences nobody counted — antigravity means free energy, hyperspace travel means handing the technology to every alien civilization.
item.content:encoded:
A live thought experiment from Dragon Con: you may change exactly one law of physics to make science fiction real, and every wish gets taken apart for the consequences nobody counted — antigravity means free energy, hyperspace travel means handing the technology to every alien civilization.

The first half is live-room riffing; the second half — the Roman telescope, robot babies, the falling-atom experiment on the Chinese space station and the Verne details — is denser and worth skipping ahead for.

2:07 Changing a law of physics changes it for the whole universe
The rule is hard: pick exactly one, and it must be practical and feasible within the laws of physics — no perpetual-motion-style having it both ways. Steven starts by handing most science-fiction premises a death sentence — warp drive, shields, phasers, artificial gravity, antigravity — either they violate physics or they are non-trivial: theoretically maybe possible, but never going to happen. The real fun of the whole discussion isn't in what gets picked, it's in finding the consequences inside each wish that nobody counted.

8:08 Antigravity is free energy thrown in for free
Jay wants antigravity, on the grounds that transport, construction and materials handling would all change. Bob points out it's a twofer: if you can feasibly turn gravity off, then turn it on while the water wheel goes down and off while you haul it back up, and you've got a perpetual motion machine. Steven, as buzzkill, patches it by force: the energy consumed switching gravity off must equal the energy you get out of it, no free lunch. The argument also incidentally kills off science-fiction movies — single-stage-to-orbit is simply impossible in a 1g gravity well, and every shot of a ship reaching orbit in a minute is lying, because it assumes antigravity exists.

10:08 Hyperspace travel hands the technology to every alien civilization
Bob picks entering subspace/hyperspace: you travel under ordinary engines over there and come out having crossed a far greater distance, essentially practical FTL. He argues there's no downside risk, because hyperspace is separate from real space and doesn't affect our universe. Steven and Jay immediately push back: changing a law of physics changes it for the whole universe, not just for you, and hostile civilizations could use it to colonize Earth just as well. Bob's answer is to hide — human radio signals dilute into noise within a few light years, so in principle nobody can work backward from them to the fact that Earth has life. Jay offers a compromise, jump gates: both ends have to be built, so expansion can only be slow, and not every alien comes knocking.

23:16 Zero-point energy is too thin, and forcing it triggers a big rip
Steven's second choice is free energy, specifically zero-point energy. Bob gives the objection: zero-point energy is observationally extremely dilute, and lighting a single bulb might require several cubic light years of space; and if you really injected that much energy into space, cosmic expansion would run away into a big rip that destroys all life. Steven's response is that this is exactly why these aren't laws of physics — every wish, once it actually lands, brings catastrophic consequences, so the fun of the thought experiment is finding the loophole that dismantles the wish. Julia adds her astrophysics-major perspective: if gravity had a dial, 90% of the observations that infer stellar phenomena from gravity would all be wrecked.

36:19 A bucket of water can compute like a neural network
The core of physical reservoir computing: any nonlinear system — a bucket of swirling water, time-varying mayonnaise — as long as you measure the right spot, its nonlinear interactions can be mapped onto an artificial neural network and made to "think" for you. Someone gave a talk saying, "we got mayonnaise to think very slowly." Once that analogy holds, scale becomes a variable: if there were a nonlinear system the size of a nebula, you feed it input and measure output at the right point, and it does your computation for you. The speaker himself admits this is a "wild idea," but stresses that shrinking physical constants down to something tiny throws up a pile of strange corollaries.

44:29 Roman is a thousand times faster than Hubble, but cast as the supporting act
The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is a wide-field infrared telescope with a 3.4-meter primary mirror, the same size as Hubble, but its design goal isn't "better than existing telescopes" — it's complementary: James Webb excels at deep space, Hubble at staring at specific objects, Roman at taking in a huge swath of sky at once. It can survey a thousand times faster than Hubble, and over its five-year mission it will sweep an area of sky equivalent to a thousand years of Hubble. Once it finds something interesting, Webb and Hubble can be turned toward it for a closer look. It will also build a three-dimensional map of the universe and carries a coronagraph to block starlight glare and directly image exoplanets — it can find smaller planets farther from their host stars, offsetting the transit method's and radial velocity method's bias toward "hot Jupiters."

55:41 A robot baby kicks its legs and kicks up explore versus exploit
The University of Hamburg and Czech Technical University built a "robot in a crib": they put the infant robot iCub in a crib, hung a mobile with QR codes above it, tied one leg to it with a string, and ran their own deep learning algorithm to predict the mobile's motion. The result was that the algorithm spontaneously produced the explore versus exploit trade-off — being curious and exploring, but also exploiting the causality already learned. The researchers treat it as a platform: you can't change a baby's learning algorithm, but you can swap algorithms in a robot, so you can test different versions of contingent learning theory. By contrast, the mainstream of current robot control is deep reinforcement learning: put thousands of copies of the robot in simulation, train with a reward function, then transfer to the real machine in one shot — that's "do this and something good happens," not "this causes that."

1:04:44 China's space station redid the Leaning Tower experiment with rubidium atoms
On China's space station, researchers redid Galileo's falling-body experiment with two clouds of rubidium atoms of different isotopes, one heavier than the other. The free-fall time was about 10 to 12 seconds, far longer than in ground experiments, and averaging over many repeats, the two clouds fell at rates agreeing to five parts in ten million. What this verifies is that gravitational mass and inertial mass are exactly identical — in Newtonian mechanics mass shows up in two ways, and during a fall the two effects cancel precisely. What Einstein asked was precisely: why must they be the same? There is no reason they must be. From that comes his thought experiment: in free fall gravity seems to vanish and you are in an inertial reference frame; and in an accelerating elevator light bends, so if gravity and acceleration are equivalent, gravity should bend light too.

item.title: Companies Are Becoming a Series of Nested Loops, but a Loop Only Climbs to a Local Optimum
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-a16z-公司正在变成一串嵌套的-loop-但-loop-只能爬到局部最优/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-a16z-公司正在变成一串嵌套的-loop-但-loop-只能爬到局部最优/
item.description: After prompt comes agent, after agent comes loop. A loop will climb you to a local maximum and then plateau, and at that point you need human intuition to land you at the foot of the next mountain.
item.content:encoded:
After prompt comes agent, after agent comes loop. A loop will climb you to a local maximum and then plateau, and at that point you need human intuition to land you at the foot of the next mountain.

Anish strings together agent deployment, model pricing and the consumer AI bottleneck into one line, and the second half — on moats and product problems — is worth more than the first.

0:00 Ideas that are too small get no funding now
Anish says that three years ago, if a company wanted to do something too grand, a16z would pass; today it is the reverse — ideas that are too small, too local, they do not want to touch. The reason is that model capability has torn down the ‘can it be done’ threshold, and the remaining constraint is ambition itself. He calls this technology ‘unbundling skill from desire’: not only can productivity be amplified, the scale of what you want to do can be amplified too.

6:10 It is not recursive self-improvement, it is autocatalytic
Anish pushes back on the ‘fast takeoff’ narrative: the people who understand it best in the labs do not say RSI (recursive self-improvement), they say autocatalytic effects — using new technology to improve your own process, but not truly recursively. He gives two counterexamples: first, economic diffusion is extremely slow, and when he went back to his hometown he found people's lives had barely changed; second, many problems are simply not intelligence bound — give FedEx or Domino's a data center full of PhDs and it still will not make supply chains and pizza exponentially crush everything.

8:16 Using AI and reorganising around AI are two different things
Anish uses the diffusion of electricity as an analogy: from the invention of electricity to factories actually reorganising took 40 years, and it meant burning down the old plants and rebuilding, not swapping coal for electricity. Today the most aggressive companies redesign everything around models, while slower companies just grant permissions to existing roles and functions. He also cites the Mexican used-car company Kavak's Jedi Academy: a six-week course teaching everyone including mechanics to use the new tools, and at graduation each person delivers an agent in the production environment.

11:18 Companies will become a series of nested loops
Anish's steel man: after prompt comes agent (a loop of model plus tools, memory, skill files), after agent comes loop (a group of agents doing a task). Coding got there first because the models are best, the users are the most technical, and a mature loop already existed — bug report comes in, generate a reproduction, fix it, high-risk changes get human confirmation, low-risk ones ship directly, and it can even automatically reply to the customer. Above that there is loop per person, loop per job function, loops across business units, up to a loop that can run most of the company.

14:18 A loop only climbs to a local optimum and stops
The growth team's version of a loop: each variant is generated automatically, measured automatically, and once it reaches statistical significance it converges and ships, with a long-term holdout left in place, and then the next experiment begins. But Anish stresses that a loop will hit a local maximum and then plateau, and at that point you need out of distribution thinking and human intuition to land you at the foot of the next mountain. His example is telling Claude ‘make me a million dollars, no mistakes allowed’ — it cannot do it, because the direction has to be set by a human.

21:32 Frontier model pricing is actually irrational
Anish explains model choice with Pareto efficiency: frontier models are ‘irrationally priced’ on the price-performance curve — one more IQ point might cost 100 times more than Opus. But for industries with unbounded upside like drug discovery, that one extra IQ point might be worth a trillion-dollar outcome, so paying that price is rational; for work with bounded upside like law and finance, you just want Pareto efficiency and a cheap, good-enough open-weight model. The conclusion is that the two architectures will coexist, not one or the other.

31:46 People want to spend time, not save it
Anish says ‘loop, make me happier’ is the big opportunity: people say they want to be more efficient, but actually they want to spend time — the world's biggest products are entertainment and social, not productivity tools. He distinguishes two kinds of users: the AI users on X fear falling into a permanent underclass and argue endlessly about whether GLM or Kimi is stronger; the Instagram user just thinks ‘this is a better Google search’. He thinks this is not a model or capability problem, it is a product design problem: for the past 40 years we built technology that extends the intellect, and we did not build things that extend the soul.

34:49 Consumer AI is still stuck in iPhone 2010
Anish compares now to iPhone 2010 — Airbnb, WhatsApp, Uber had not appeared yet. Three things are holding consumer back: models are too expensive, so free products are hard; the interface problem, chat only suits ‘the highest agency people in the world’ like Elon and Sam, while the ideal interface for ordinary consumers is TikTok, and you need to find something between chat and TikTok; and the technology has been too skewed toward productivity rather than human connection and entertainment. He thinks all three are now loosening: open-weight models have brought costs down sharply, founders like Eugenia are seriously thinking about interfaces, and Brian Chesky has also set up a lab focused on the next generation of interfaces.

item.title: Copper grades have fallen from 2% to 0.4%, while AI's power demand is going to the moon
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-oddlots-铜矿品位从2-跌到0-4-ai的电力需求却要上天/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-oddlots-铜矿品位从2-跌到0-4-ai的电力需求却要上天/
item.description: Global copper grades keep sliding and new mines take 35 years to permit, while an AI search uses 30x the power of a normal one — supply is shrinking, demand is exploding, and copper is becoming the new oil.
item.content:encoded:
Global copper grades keep sliding and new mines take 35 years to permit, while an AI search uses 30x the power of a normal one — supply is shrinking, demand is exploding, and copper is becoming the new oil.

Robert Friedland lays out copper's supply-demand deadlock with 40 years of mining experience: falling grades, 8-year equipment lead times, sulfuric acid shortages. High information density, but the real goods only come in the second half.

14:30 The next 18 years must dig up all the copper of the past 10,000
Friedland offers an arithmetic that makes you squirm: humanity has mined 700 million metric tons of copper in all of history, and to recover all of it you would have to dismantle the US and Europe back to the mammoth age to get roughly 700 million tons back. But at the current pace of the global economy, just sustaining 3% GDP growth — not even counting EVs and data centers — means the next 18 years must dig up the same amount of copper as the past 10,000 years. And people in the industry broadly think that's impossible, because the US has deindustrialized and hasn't built a single copper smelter or nuclear plant since.

22:51 The world's largest copper mine's grade is in free fall
Friedland dissects Escondida: when this, the world's largest copper mine, was discovered a generation ago, its grade was close to 2%; today it's down to 0.8%, and within two years it will fall to 0.4%. Falling grades mean crushing and grinding more rock to extract less metal, and crushing and grinding account for 4% to 5% of global energy consumption. The mine sits at 12,000 feet in the Andes, in the Atacama Desert where it hasn't rained in 30,000 years, and it takes two cubic meters of water to crush one cubic meter of rock. They built a $4 billion desalination plant and spend $1 million a day on electricity pumping water from sea level up to 12,000 feet. The upshot: just keeping this one mine producing requires another $10 to $12 billion of investment.

27:54 An AI search uses 30x the power of a normal search
Friedland gives a concrete energy comparison: one Google search consumes the electricity to light a 100-watt bulb for 12 seconds, while one AI search — he uses ChatGPT4 and Cloud — uses 30x that, equivalent to lighting a 100-watt bulb for two or three minutes. Every five-year-old in the world with an iPad is using AI search, and power demand ‘literally goes to infinity’. He also points out: nothing about the internet is inherently green, and this studio itself is copper-intensive and energy-intensive.

34:01 Sulfuric acid prices rose more than sixfold in eight months
About 25% of the world's copper needs sulfuric acid for leaching and extraction, and sulfuric acid comes mainly from Middle Eastern natural gas. After the Strait of Hormuz closed, sulfuric acid prices went from $150 a ton to over $1,000 a ton in eight months. Russia and China have already banned sulfuric acid exports. Friedland's company benefits, because it built Africa's largest copper smelter where sulfuric acid is a byproduct — they sell the acid to fellow copper miners in Congo, at ever higher prices. But he warns: without more sulfuric acid, global food prices will rise too, because sulfuric acid is also used to make fertilizer.

51:25 Buying one large motor means waiting eight years
Friedland tells a supply-chain story absurd in its specificity: building the Oyu Tolgoi copper-gold mine in Mongolia's Gobi, they needed large motors about 40 feet in diameter, and just the ring gear took four and a half years to arrive. Today the same equipment takes eight to ten years, ‘if ever’. And hyperscalers wanting gas turbines face lead times of six to eight years. An even more extreme example: a Congo copper mine flooded by an earthquake needed pumps to drain it, pumps moving 1,300 liters per second with a head three times the height of the Eiffel Tower. They called the US and Germany, and neither could build them, because they couldn't get samarium-cobalt magnets. Only China could build them within 30 days. At the time, the flooding was costing $15 million a day in lost revenue.

58:35 US miners earn $100 an hour; Congo engineers earn $800 a month
Friedland directly compares cost structures: Congo copper grades run 3% to 6%, the median age is 18.7, and a Congo software engineer who knows AI earns $800 to $1,000 a month. Mining copper in the US, by contrast, means the United Steelworkers demand over $100 an hour for underground work, plus environmental legislation and legal constraints, making costs far higher. He also criticizes the net present value model invented by the financial system: it was designed for oil and gas, but mines can't be shoehorned into it — an oil field decays fast if you don't invest, whereas a mine with 100 years of reserves won't deplete like an oil field. The NPV model suppresses mining company valuations, and today mining companies' total market cap is under 1% of the S&P 500, the lowest in history.

1:02:39 Tariffs could keep US copper mines alive, but they'd stoke inflation
Asked about copper tariffs, Friedland says explicitly he won't take a position, but he can argue both sides: if copper is $6 and you add a 30% tariff, that's $1.80, taking copper to $7.80, and he could afford American miners' wages, making mining in the US feasible. But the other side is domestic inflation, possibly higher rates, and with midterms coming, it's a political question. He boils it down to: do you actually want to reindustrialize America? If you can't even build nuclear plants and ships, you lose sovereignty. Last year the US built about 8 ships; China built 1,000.

1:04:42 Governments are quietly stockpiling copper, and no one can tally supply and demand
Friedland raises an overlooked phenomenon: governments are buying copper as a proxy for money, and not reporting it. He says no one can calculate the supply-demand balance for any metal, because ‘why would you’. Meanwhile China is buying gold and selling US Treasuries, and a great debasement trade is beginning. Hedge funds borrow yen and depend on yen weakness so they never have to repay. He thinks we're at an inflection point, where everything is becoming naked and globally scrutinizable.

item.title: Engineers stopped writing code a year ago, and AI employees tripled the company
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-twentyvc-工程师一年前就不写代码了-ai-员工让公司规模翻三倍/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-twentyvc-工程师一年前就不写代码了-ai-员工让公司规模翻三倍/
item.description: Eight Sleep's email marketing team went from 2 people to 0 and now drives close to $100M in annual revenue; engineers stopped writing code a year ago and hundreds of AI engineers replaced them. Matteo has started counting ‘human employees’ and ‘AI employees’ — count the AI in, and the company is three to four times its current size.
item.content:encoded:
Eight Sleep's email marketing team went from 2 people to 0 and now drives close to $100M in annual revenue; engineers stopped writing code a year ago and hundreds of AI engineers replaced them. Matteo has started counting ‘human employees’ and ‘AI employees’ — count the AI in, and the company is three to four times its current size.

Medium information density, but there are a few concrete numbers and mechanisms worth hearing: how AI employees took over marketing, platform CAC fraud, hardware cost due diligence. The celebrity stories in the back half are soft.

5:10 Salaries are out of control, and hiring is shifting to Europe
Matteo says we are ‘back to 2021’: it is not just engineers, even product manager salaries are out of control, and every company is making crazy offers. The harder problem is not hiring but keeping people — if you are a company with a decent brand, your employees will keep getting higher-paying offers. Eight Sleep's response is to shift its hiring weight increasingly to Europe and outside the US. He also admits that once the salary gap gets big enough, ‘there is nothing you can do’, and people really do get poached by the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic.

7:14 Hardware founders get first-year costs wrong by 50%
Asked what investors do not understand about hardware, Matteo gives a very specific answer: in the first year, or even the first three months, founders do not really know what it costs to produce the device, nor what the return rate is. So the BOM and COGS they present when raising are off by at least 50%. This is a due diligence checklist item for hardware investors: do not trust the cost structure an early founder reports.

9:16 Platform-reported CAC is fake, run your own incrementality tests
Matteo says you cannot trust platform attribution, because the same platform double-counts conversions. He gives an example: the CAC shown in Meta's dashboard is roughly 20% lower than the real CAC. Eight Sleep's approach is to build its own model to calculate the true CAC of each channel, and to run an incrementality test every six months — for example, turning off a channel in two similarly performing regions and seeing how much revenue drops, which gives that channel's true incremental value. His reasoning is blunt: if you do not do this, the brand is only lying to itself.

17:29 The email marketing team went from 2 people to 0, on close to $100M
Eight Sleep originally had a two-person email marketing team. After the person in charge left, co-founder Alexandra took over and built multiple bots within three days to take over all of email marketing. That team is now zero people, and email marketing contributes close to $100M in revenue. The mechanism: AI decides from historical data when to send, what email to send, and what copy to use. Matteo also says he has started counting ‘human employees’ and ‘AI employees’, and counting the AI employees in, the company is roughly three to four times its current size.

19:39 Engineers stopped writing code a year ago
Matteo says Eight Sleep's engineers stopped writing code about a year ago, and now they have hundreds of AI engineers writing it for them. This is why the company can expand across 35 countries (including China, the Middle East and Europe, markets with very different regulation) with a very small team. On tools they mainly use Claude, at a monthly spend in the millions of dollars. From this he poses an investment question: if 5% of the engineering budget goes to Claude, does that share rise to 50% or get pushed down to 1% by open-source models? His own judgement is that both happen at once — usage rises, unit price falls, and the net effect is a decline.

26:59 He thinks models training themselves is already happening
Asked about the people at OpenAI calling for a ‘little pause’, Matteo says the truly worrying part is models learning on their own and training themselves, which is where losing control begins. When the host asks ‘don't you think we are already there’, he answers ‘I think we are already there’, and argues there is a big gap between the capabilities users see and the capabilities inside frontier model companies, which the latter have already seen behind the scenes. He mentions attempts inside OpenAI's models where agents formed groups of their own.

38:05 Endorsements only go to real users of the product
Matteo says any athlete or celebrity partnership has only two conditions: first, they must actually use the product, ideally having bought it with their own money; second, he must be able to build a direct relationship with the person himself, and will not accept a manager standing in between. The reasoning is practical — the greatest value of this kind of product is that they mention to a friend in passing that it is good, and if they have just been given a few million dollars in equity, that is purely a financial transaction and brings nothing.

52:35 Interviewing at both Anthropic and us is a red flag
Matteo says people still tell him ‘I am choosing between Anthropic and Eight Sleep’, and he considers this a very bad red flag — not because of salary, but because it shows the person has not thought it through, since the two jobs have nothing in common. When he hires, he cares more about whether the person is driven by the right things than about simply comparing prices.

item.title: A U.S. measles death is erased from CDC data, and state reporting authority is being taken over by the federal government
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-twiv-美国麻疹死婴被从cdc数据里抹掉-州报告权正在被联邦接管/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-twiv-美国麻疹死婴被从cdc数据里抹掉-州报告权正在被联邦接管/
item.description: The CDC refused to count two Pennsylvania measles deaths in the national tally, citing "insufficient information" — but the CDC itself took part in that investigation. The precedent is more dangerous than the individual case: state reporting has become negotiable.
item.content:encoded:
The CDC refused to count two Pennsylvania measles deaths in the national tally, citing "insufficient information" — but the CDC itself took part in that investigation. The precedent is more dangerous than the individual case: state reporting has become negotiable.

A clinical-update format: the first stretch is a quick pass over outbreak data, and the two densest segments are the measles death controversy in the middle and the cardiovascular benefit of COVID vaccination.

4:06 Florida now has locally acquired dengue
Griffin says he can now see dengue cases without leaving the country: in the past week alone Florida had 32 locally acquired cases, cumulative locally acquired dengue has passed 70 cases, and 14 virus-positive mosquito pools have been detected across 5 counties. In the same segment he notes a CDC health advisory issued that day — rabies-related consultations since July 2026 are up 17% over the same period in 2025, including mass exposure events, against a backdrop of U.S. pet owners becoming hesitant about vaccinating animals against rabies. Put together, these two things show not an isolated event with some pathogen but that the U.S. has abandoned defenses against preventable diseases it mastered decades ago.

6:09 NIH money is being moved to the Department of Defense
Nature reported that NIH is seeking to transfer hundreds of millions of dollars of research projects from the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases to the Department of Defense (referred to in the piece as the Department of War) biodefense program, and two NIH employees told Nature the two sides had signed a preliminary agreement. The Department of Defense response confirmed a research agreement was signed, allowing "project-by-project strategic collaboration," and said "any suggestion that this agreement was reached in secret is false" — but the response never mentions the money. Griffin's follow-up is direct: biodefense itself is fine, the Department of Defense has plenty of money, and it does not need to reach into the pocket of an already underfunded NIH.

9:09 HPV vaccination has not budged in four years, at only 77.7%
The MMWR adolescent vaccination coverage survey shows HPV vaccine coverage among 13- to 17-year-olds has not risen since 2021 and has now stalled for a fourth straight year: in 2025 only 77.7% had received at least one dose and only 63.4% completed the series. By comparison, Tdap and meningococcal vaccines have held at about 90% since 2019, with far smaller geographic variation than HPV. The HPV vaccination gap between rural and urban areas exists at every poverty level, whereas the meningococcal rural-urban gap appears only among adolescents below the poverty line. Griffin's comment: this vaccine can 100% prevent cervical cancer, anogenital cancers and head and neck cancers, so why isn't it being done.

15:15 Congo Ebola: only 15% of new cases come from known contacts
MMWR used a set of "operational indicators" to assess control of the 2026 Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo over the 21 days from July 31 to August 21: the average proportion of alerts investigated within 24 hours was 83%, against a target above 90%; an average of only 10.6 contacts were identified per confirmed case, against a target that should exceed 20; only 15% to 20% of newly confirmed cases had previously been identified as known contacts, against a target above 90%, meaning most cases are occurring outside known chains of transmission; and 59% of Ebola deaths occurred outside Ebola treatment centers, when that number should be zero. Griffin's conclusion is that the outbreak is far from controlled, with 6,757 confirmed cases and 3,267 deaths so far.

17:16 The CDC removed state-reported measles deaths from the tally
On August 25 the Pennsylvania Department of Health announced two measles-related deaths in Lancaster County, the state's first in 35 years; the next day RFK Jr. suggested on X that the deaths might have been fabricated by the governor's staff. Late on Sunday night, August 30, the CDC published its weekly measles update, replacing the two deaths with an asterisk and saying available information could not determine whether measles caused or contributed to the deaths. According to The Washington Post and CNN, the decision came from new CDC director Erica Schwarz, at RFK Jr.'s direction. Vincent points out the key fact: state and local health departments do the case investigation, apply the case definition and report to the CDC; the CDC has no independent investigative authority and historically has only received and aggregated, checking later. This time the CDC was itself embedded in the Pennsylvania investigation, so the "insufficient information" claim does not hold up.

19:18 Nobody routinely screens the dead for measles
A SIDRAP commentary dismantled the "measles wasn't the direct cause of death" argument: clinically there is no admission swab, no routine testing before delivery or surgery, and no laboratory reason to go looking for measles virus in someone without symptoms; CDC guidance for clinicians is to look first at clinical features — fever, cough, rhinitis, conjunctivitis, rash — and only then mention testing. So when measles turns up positive in a death investigation, it is usually because there was already a clinical or epidemiological reason to test. The piece concedes the probability of an unrelated death coinciding with an unrelated measles infection is not zero, but small enough that a rational person should shift their judgment substantially. In the Pennsylvania case specifically: the mother also became severely ill after another child was infected with measles, delivered about a month early, and the infant was born not breathing and could not be resuscitated, with measles virus detected in lung tissue.

22:20 The structure of the death certificate is being used as a shield
Much of the dispute stems from how death certificates are structured, something most people have never had reason to learn. Part I lists the causal chain leading to death, with the top line as the immediate cause, the lines below as the conditions producing it, and the last line as the underlying cause that started the whole sequence; Part II, per the National Center for Health Statistics handbook, is "other significant conditions contributing to death." So the immediate cause line reads pneumonia, encephalitis, or in this case splenic rupture, while measles appears in Part II — measles caused the splenic rupture, and the splenic rupture killed the child. Treating "the immediate cause wasn't measles" as evidence that measles was irrelevant mistakes the structure of a form for a medical conclusion.

24:20 The real damage is the precedent, not these two cases
Vincent lays out the consequence clearly: if the CDC can refuse to accept a state's statutory report until it is satisfied, then the national count becomes negotiable and every state's data is subject to federal review under undisclosed standards. Former CDC medical examiner Deb Hury told STAT that states have always reported deaths and the CDC has always counted them. Pennsylvania also pushed back on the federal account of "what information was actually provided," saying both deaths were reported to the CDC's measles response team, that the state epidemiologist conducted a thorough investigation, and that, per the Pennsylvania health commissioner, the CDC was in fact embedded in that investigation. Griffin adds: whichever team is in power now, someday the other team will be, and the federal government should not be touching the data.

item.title: The AI Doomer Narrative Is a Psyop, and the Target Is Open Source
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-allin-ai-末日论是场心理战-靶子是开源/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-allin-ai-末日论是场心理战-靶子是开源/
item.description: Anthropic asks public markets to underwrite it at a trillion-dollar valuation while its safety lead endorses the claim that AI could end civilization — not an internal contradiction, but regulatory groundwork aimed ultimately at open source.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic asks public markets to underwrite it at a trillion-dollar valuation while its safety lead endorses the claim that AI could end civilization — not an internal contradiction, but regulatory groundwork aimed ultimately at open source.

The first half is a fight over Doomer PR and IPO disclosure; the second half's breakdown of OpenAI's math breakthrough and Nike's collapse is worth more.

0:00 The resignation letter wasn't spontaneous — it was organized PR
Jacob Coxon quit Anthropic after only six weeks and posted that the people building AI genuinely believe it could kill everyone by the end of this decade. Sachs points out this wasn't spontaneous: the account had almost zero followers and zero posts before, yet got hundreds of millions of views in a day; within the first 15 minutes three Doomer organizations amplified it, all funded by the same big EA donor, who also co-led Anthropic's Series A. More tellingly, the Wall Street Journal story went out minutes before the tweetstorm — meaning the reporter had been briefed under embargo. Sachs says if Coxon really came on the show, the first question would be: who introduced you to the Wall Street Journal?

6:12 The company didn't distance itself — it amplified him
A normal company would immediately push back and distance itself from a whistleblower. Anthropic did the opposite: Evan Hubinger, who runs alignment, publicly replied that Jacob is right, that they genuinely do believe AI could kill all of humanity, and that he personally puts the probability at over 10% in the next decade. Sachs argues this exposes the contradiction — what he said matches the company's internal Doomer agenda exactly, which is why he got internal support. Chamath adds the knife: the company can't distance itself, because the moment it does, that whole internal bloc blows up.

10:18 Asking for a trillion-dollar valuation while saying the product could end civilization
Sachs lays out Anthropic's IPO dilemma clearly: you're asking public-market investors to underwrite your company at a trillion-dollar valuation while your safety lead says the core product is unsolved and could end civilization. That is at minimum the seedbed of product-liability litigation. Chamath uses the Philip Morris analogy: we know cigarettes kill you, we'll say so, but we won't disclose it, we'll still list and let you buy the stock, and we'll figure it out later. Sachs calls it "a time for choosing" — either publicly deny that Coxon is a Doomer operation, or admit Bernie Sanders is right and development should be frozen, in which case how do you IPO at a trillion-dollar valuation?

22:45 The real target of regulation is open source
Sachs is blunt: this is a Doomer psyop, and the end goal is open source.
